speechtext: MEMBER FOR JOLIETTE-l/ASSOMPTION-MONTCALM

subtopic: MR. SPEAKER  STATEMENT ON QUESTION BY
speechtext:
On Friday morning the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) rose on a question of privilege respecting certain statements made by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Francis) the previous day. His declaration was to the effect that the hon. member had said about him things that were untrue or false. The words used in French were "des choses fausses". After quite a debate had taken place I said that I would examine the matter over the week end and give a decision on Monday; that is today.
There are evidently two questions which arise. The first and most important one is the question of privilege, and the second one is whether an expression used by the hon. member was unparliamentary. I will deal first with the latter, as it will soon be disposed of. The hon. member, speaking in French, stated;

The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Francis) said some false things about me. He took advantage of my absence to do so.

It was then I stated that the use of the term "false" is not parliamentary. I had not realized at that moment that the word "false" was applied to things said and not to the hon. member for Carleton. If one hon. member should say of another hon. member that he was a liar, or that he had affirmed something knowing that such a thing was untrue, this of course would be unparliamentary. However, this is not the same as saying that what a member says of another member is not true.
Having disposed of one part of the incident, I should perhaps take advantage of this occasion to deal with the question of privilege per se and I will try to do it in very general terms, in terms that will render my remarks applicable to this and to all other questions of privilege raised in this house.
There are still areas of the work of the Commons which are causing some difficulties
in reference to procedure. This may be the understatement of the year. One of these areas relates to questions of privilege. More and more often members are rising to invoke so-called questions of privilege which could more properly be classified as mere interruptions, ordinary points of order, untimely grievances, disguised charges, contempts, or even simple disagreements with what is being said from the floor of the house.
Hon. members rose on questions of privilege over a hundred times during the previous session of parliament. As there were 117 sitting days from May 16 when the house met to December 21 when the house prorogued, this means that invoking privilege practically became, and has continued to be, a daily occurrence. I dare say that not 10 per cent, nay 5 per cent, were proper questions of privilege. Moreover, only three or four of these were followed by a motion which would have been the proper procedure to adopt in the circumstances.
As a sample of what I have stated, early Friday morning the hon. member rose twice on a question of privilege, the first time to the effect that it was his "duty to direct questions to the Prime Minister and to any member of the cabinet"; and he added "If I am out of order, Mr. Speaker, it is your responsibility to deal with the matter and I shall abide by your ruling, provided it is fair and reasonable". This last comment was perhaps unnecessary, and it was not a question of privilege in any event.
As may be seen if one takes the trouble to read citations 108 to 112 of Beauchesne's parliamentary rules, privilege is a very serious matter and therefore should not be abused. I might perhaps terminate the present statement by directing the attention of the house to one particular quotation from Beauchesne which is to be found at page 102, a quotation which should be read carefully by all members as it summarizes the situation clearly and without equivocation. This is the quotation:
113. Members often raise so-called "questions of privilege" on matters which should be dealt with as personal explanations or corrections, either in the debates or the proceedings of the house. A question of privilege ought rarely to come up in parliament. It should be dealt with by a motion giving the house power to impose a reparation or apply a remedy. There are privileges of the house as well as of members individually. Wilful disobedience to orders and rules of parliament in the exercise of its constitutional functions; insults and obstructions during debate are breaches of the

Question of Privilege
privileges of the house. Libels upon members and aspersions upon them in relation to parliament and interference of any kind with their official duties, are breaches of the privileges of the members. But a dispute arising between two members, as to allegations of facts, does not fulfil the conditions of parliamentary privilege. An attack in a newspaper article is not a breach of privilege, unless it comes within the definition of privileges above given, and then a member is bound to lay on the table the newspaper in which the article complained of appears-

MR. NIELSEN  REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MINISTER OP JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege. I feel I must do so because I did give the house notice last Friday that I intended to raise this question.
The question is one which involves two separate factors, one concerning the translation from English to French, and second the translation from French to English as relayed by the translators in the translation booths. Most of the time these translators do an excellent service to the house, but in this particular debate last Thursday they did break down for a moment. I have not, of course, access to the blues in the Hansard office, but on page 1964 of Hansard for Thursday last, about half way down the right hand column, the Minister of Justice is reported as using these words:
I say that the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), who is perhaps the one who most bitterly criticized the attitude of the government in the house, has always intimated something which is false both in fact and in law.
Then a little further on in the same column he said:
I say that such statements are a hateful betrayal of the truth, of the facts and of the law.
I have checked with several of my colleagues on this side of the house, Mr. Speaker, and all confirm me in my recollection that the translation which came over the earphones in English was as follows:
I say that an hon. member of this house who has most bitterly attacked the government-
-and then followed the remainder of the text. So the English translation did not specifically name me at the time. Had that occurred, Mr. Speaker, I would have risen, probably at the stage where the minister used the words:
I say that such statements are a hateful betrayal of the truth-
-and so on. So the first point involved in this question of privilege is one of an English translation coming over the system possibly quite different from the words the minister actually used, or any other hon. member actually used. The other factor involved in the

privilege is the words used themselves. Without having had the opportunity to study in detail the statement Your Honour made today, I have not come to a conclusion as to whether or not these words, in the context of your ruling, are parliamentary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: MR. NIELSEN  REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MINISTER OP JUSTICE
speechtext:
On a point of order, so long as the hon. member was referring to the fact that the translation of my words may not have been accurate, I was not personally concerned and I allowed the hon. member for Yukon to deal with his question of privilege. But I contend now that so long as he intends to raise a question of privilege, in my respect, of course that is ruled out by Your Honour's previous ruling. But even if it were not, so long as the hon. member purports to raise a question of privilege based on the utterances of any hon. member of the house, and in the present instance utterances by me, I say that Your Honour may not entertain any discussion except on the basis of the original text for which I must take responsibility, that is the text in which I made my remarks, the French text.
This is the only text that can be opposed to me. If the hon. member is ready to discuss the question on the basis of the French text itself and to say I may have used words which are not parliamentary, then I might be in a better position to answer him, but I say that on the basis of the translation he cannot confront me with the words in the translation.

maintopic: MR. NIELSEN  REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MINISTER OP JUSTICE
speechtext:
I can clear up that question at the outset, on the point of order raised by the Minister of Justice. I have examined both texts and have consulted with some of my French speaking colleagues, and both texts in Hansard show that the minister did use words identifying me in his remarks. I do not question at all that any alterations have been made in Hansard. That was my original suspicion, but since both texts coincide I simply have to conclude that the mistake itself was made in the translation from the French to the English.
Now, to proceed with this second factor in the point of privilege I raised, as my authority for perhaps questioning the words used by the Minister of Justice I merely cite the Minister of Transport who, as recorded at page 1197 of Friday's Hansard, said:
-that when one hon. member undertakes to suggest that another hon. member has said something that is false, it is up to him to prove it was a false statement by real evidence, and not simply to use an unparliamentary word as a form of innuendo.
And I believe Your Honour, as recorded at the same page of Hansard, said that the term "false" was not parliamentary. This may have been changed in view of Your Honour's

ruling today, but without having studied it carefully I would not be in a position to venture an opinion. I merely draw to Your Honour's attention these words which the minister used as recorded at page 1964 of Hansard for Thursday last, April 9:
I say that the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen)... has always intimated something which is false both in fact and in law-
I say that such statements are a hateful betrayal of the truth-

speechtext:
1.	Did F.B.I. officers act as police officers In Canada in the Wasylenchuk case?

3.	Was Wasylenchuk transferred from the prison to the U.S.A. by Canadian officers or by the F.B.I.?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: WASYLENCHUK CASE PROCEDURE
speechtext:
1. The extradition warrant, which was in the form prescribed by the Extradition Act, directed the keeper of Oakalla prison farm to deliver John Wasylenchuk into the custody of Dean G. Rolston and Alfred G. Gunn and commanded the said Dean G. Bolston and Alfred G. Gunn to convey John Wasylenchuk to the United States. In accordance with the practice Dean G. Rolston and Alfred G. Gunn were designated for this purpose by the United States authorities. They are agents of the federal bureau of investigation.
2.	Yes.
3.	Wasylenchuk was transferred from the prison to the United States by the F.B.I. agents abovementioned who were accompanied by members of the R.C.M. Police.
4.	Prison officials at Oakalla prison farm, which is a provincial institution, have informed the R.C.M. Police that John Wasylenchuk was held at the Oakalla prison farm from October 18 to December 18, 1963, awaiting his extradition, upon which latter date he was delivered to the F.B.I. agents, as above described, and that during this time he received approximately 20 visits from relatives, friends, parole officers, members of the John Howard society and a priest.

subtopic: *QUEBEC PROJECTS TO RELIEVE UNEMPLOYMENT
*QUEBEC PROJECTS TO RELIEVE UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: What new projects does the government intend to carry out in order to eliminate unemployment in the province of Quebec particularly?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: *QUEBEC PROJECTS TO RELIEVE UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: The government has developed and introduced a number of programs designed to strengthen the economy generally and to bring about an adequate growth in employment. The effectiveness of these programs can be seen from the fact that employment in the past five months has averaged some 270,000 higher than in the corresponding period of the year before and is over 90,000 higher in Quebec. Unemployment has averaged about 60,000 lower for Canada and about 20,000 lower in Quebec. The government has strengthened employment in the winter months which has resulted in seasonal unemployment being significantly lower this winter than in previous winters through the winter house building program and an expanded municipal winter works incentive program. New programs, as they are developed for dealing with unemployment, will be announced to parliament in the usual way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

speechtext: Did the Postmaster General, during November last, agree to open a post office in the village of Rednersville, Ontario, and, if so, when will such a post office be opened?

subtopic: POST OFFICE, REDNERSVILLE, ONT.
speechtext:
Yes. It was decided at that time that a post office closed in 1961 should be reopened at Rednersville, Ontario, in accordance with what the Postmaster General understood to be the wishes of the great

Questions
majority of patrons residing within a half a mile radius of the proposed site. At that time the Postmaster General had been given to understand that the patrons concerned generally were agreeable to giving up service through rural mail boxes and receiving their mail through the proposed post office.
However, a conflicting petition was received on the 31st day of January 1964, and it was deemed advisable to resurvey the area. A further canvass has now been completed and as a result 33 of the patrons have expressed a preference for service through the proposed office, and 32 are against such a move.
This canvass revealed that generally those persons residing within a quarter of a mile of the proposed site for the post office are in favour and those who reside further than a quarter of a mile are against the establishment of such a post office, if such action involves termination of the rural mail delivery service now being provided.
When a situation such as this occurs, it is the normal policy of the Post Office Department not to make any change in the existing arrangements because of the resulting adverse effect on the community as a whole. In the circumstances, and since the patrons of the area are being adequately provided with rural mail delivery service, it has been decided not to proceed with the establishment of an office at Rednersville.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with reference to the first matter, on behalf of the minister I thank the hon. member and I will bring the letter to her attention. The minister will no doubt reply to it in the house.
As far as the second matter, concerning the Miller bay Indian hospital, is concerned,

I would reply as follows. The Miller bay Indian hospital is not and never was intended to be an acute general hospital. It has been operated for the past 18 years as a 147 bed hospital for tuberculous Indians. Acute general care for British Columbia Indians has been provided in community general hospitals, through British Columbia hospital insurance services, on the same terms and conditions a their non-Indian neighbours.
Because of the progressive reduction in the Indian tuberculosis case load, the department hopes to be able to phase out the hospital's tuberculosis function over the next two or three years. Planning has been complicated by an acute bed shortage in Prince Rupert general hospital. Because general care beds are not always available for them in Prince Rupert, Miller bay has, for the past several years, been admitting local Indians urgently requiring general hospital care. When and if extra beds are available in Prince Rupert, these emergency beds in Miller bay will no longer be required and the department can proceed with the planned phase out of the tuberculosis institution.
Miller bay Indian hospital has played an important role in the department's antituberculosis program for British Columbia Indians. It is, however, a former R.C.A.F. hospital of temporary wartime construction, and the buildings are rapidly nearing the end of their useful life. Inasmuch as the remaining Indian hospitals at Nanaimo and Sardis can now carry the full Indian tuberculosis case load, there will be no justification for the continuance of this substandard treatment facility.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 24, consideration of the motion of Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance), that Mr. 
Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the magnetic attraction of extreme positions has been well illustrated by the debate on the budget introduced by the Minister of Finance on March 16, and now before us again today. Some speakers who have taken part in the debate have denounced the Minister of Finance, who reduced the forecast deficit by one third from that of the last two years, for not having done more to achieve a balanced budget. Others who have spoken regard the minister as strangely unenlightened because he has refused to budget for a massive deficit which could be achieved by greater expenditures or by a cut in taxes.
Now, what both groups are ignoring is that neither a balanced budget nor a massive deficit is desirable as an end of economic policy, per se. Deficit spending or tax cutting are useful ways of stimulating a stagnating economy, but they are useful only up to a certain point. Beyond that point they only inflate the supply of money or credit in circulation. Balancing the budget has a deflationary effect in an expanding economy, for it means that the quantity of money or credit in circulation is being held constant while the economy as a whole expands.
A balanced budget brought about by the simple expedient of slashing expenditures will have a depressing effect on an economy. This does not mean, of course, that balanced budgets are to be anxiously avoided. A balanced budget is desirable if it should come about as the result of an economy so prosperous that with the rates of neither altered, government revenues overtake government expenditures.
The demand for a balanced budget and the demand for a massive deficit, both of which we have heard in this debate, are red herrings. They tend to obscure the important consideration in the formation of national economic policy, namely the possibilities given to our people to earn a living. The general availability of jobs in a productive economy is what is supremely important. Balanced budgets or massive deficits are important chiefly as they influence this fundamental consideration.
The scarcity of jobs, that is unemployment, is now a regional problem, concentrated mainly in eastern Quebec and the Atlantic provinces, as the Minister of Finance told us on both March 16 and March 24. The deluge of unemployment has receded so that most of the nation is now free, but unemployment persists, albeit at reduced levels, in certain areas, and most especially in

Atlantic Canada. Consequently the approach of the government to the problem of unemployment must now be regional, and not general as a few months ago.
Those of us who come from Atlantic Canada are anxious to have our lower economic status corrected in so far as that lower economic status is the result not of nature but of laws and policies. It must be understood that we are not asking that natural resources be created by statute of this parliament, but we are asking that we be helped to overcome the special difficulties that our participation in Canada entails. These difficulties, which are basically three in number, spring from the fact that we are at the remote end of a narrow transcontinental economy rather than at the centre of a north Atlantic economic community. We are confined by tariff walls that do not help us much directly. In an age of improving transportation we are becoming relatively more and more isolated. Because of the centralized nature of Canada's savings and investment institutions, our savings have been drained away to produce prosperity elsewhere.
We would like to see freer international trade. We hope that the Kennedy round of negotiations under GATT will be highly successful. We want to see more and more economic and political co-operation among the nations of the world, and we should like to see the nations around the north Atlantic showing the way to co-operation.
But frankly, sir, we do not expect such moves to be so rapid as to free us soon from the disadvantages that pertain to our position at the extremity of Canada's national economic system. Consequently we were happy to see parliament recognize Canada's interest in the prosperity of the provinces by setting up the Atlantic development board and later by assigning funds to that board for its purposes. We are now elated that the board has set to work and is co-operating with the provinces in an exemplary way. It is co-operating with the municipalities, with the provinces and the federal government, and already it is producing results.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the hon. member not have some concern about the state of the fund the Atlantic development board has available to it at the moment, and the fact that large sums are being paid out of what appears to be a small amount of money when you consider the over-all impact this board is supposed to have on the economy? And does he not think we should have increased
The Budget-Mr. Stewart the size of the fund to indicate to the people of the area that they have no need to worry about future development?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In my view there is no question whatever but that the board should spend the money it was given, and spend it as rapidly and as efficiently as it can. I am quite sure that if the board comes back to this government and to this parliament, after having continued the record it so far has established, it will have no difficulty in acquiring more money to spend for useful purposes.
What I want to do now is simply to illustrate for the benefit of some of those members who do not come from the Atlantic area, the way in which the board has so far been useful. In December, 1962, speaking in this house, I mentioned a small town in my constituency, the town of Canso. This is a fine place, sir, with fine people. It is splendidly situated at the apex of a peninsula at the eastern end of the mainland of Nova Scotia. This peninsula protrudes out into the north Atlantic fishing grounds. When last I mentioned this town of Canso, the people were deeply discouraged. A great deal of money had been made there over the years in the fishery, but that money had been moved away to produce development elsewhere, and there had been little recapitalization locally. In fact the population had dropped by almost two thirds in the last 50 years.
However, during the last 16 months the picture has changed in Canso. An energetic company of competent fish processors has moved in; the provincial government of Nova Scotia has shown its willingness to cooperate; and the town of Canso has been willing to co-operate with the federal government. Consequently there is now planned there, the construction of what will be the most modern fish processing plant on the north American continent. In the meantime, the old plant is providing employment for the skilled workers of the community. Frankly, it is difficult to see how this would have been possible without the work of this board established by parliament, and without funds provided to that board by parliament. The future of this community has been assured. This shows what a board such as this, willing to co-operate with municipal, provincial and federal agencies, can accomplish when its members are determined to produce results. Now that a beginning has been made in Nova Scotia I confess we are anxious to see what will be done elsewhere.
In addition to the improvements in the fisheries which the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) is now planning in co-operation with the provincial fishery authorities,

The Budget-Mr. Stewart our region needs the modernization of its agriculture and of its forestry. We also need the introduction of more secondary industries. In many parts of eastern Canada, forestry and agriculture go together; they are connected as the foundation of the local economy, and the appointment of a minister whose duties embrace both these fields was, I think, a progressive move, especially when that minister is also charged with responsibility for carrying out the ARDA program. Our own attitude toward the ARDA program is one of cautious hope. Our caution springs from fear that the program will be approached with a reluctance borne of indolence and timidity. Our hope rises from an idea of what could be accomplished by way of the rehabilitation and development of large areas of our countryside if plans were formed imaginatively and carried out with zeal and energy. We wish that this parliament would hasten to confirm the minister in his new duties, for strong leadership in this field is needed immediately. We also need his leadership in the establishment of an eastern feed grain board or agency.
Last year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), recognizing the need for secondary industries in provinces such as Nova Scotia, announced that tax incentives would be provided for new industry locating in designated areas. On March 16, 1964, he announced that the date by which an industry had to be in production in order to qualify for the incentives was to be changed from December 5, 1965, to April 1, 1967. That is a good step, but tax incentives only help to create a temporarily attractive economic climate; they are seldom enough to overcome the various inertial forces, some economic and some non-economic, which are drawing secondary industries toward the central part of Canada. British and European experience, as I mentioned in this house on December 10, 1962, has shown that specific assistance in various forms-the preparation of sites and facilities, capital grants to assist construction, and financial assistance during the settling-in period, can be most effective. I realize that many of these devices are not available to a federal minister of finance. Such measures can be initiated and are most likely to succeed in co-operation with provincial governments after a thorough but not too prolonged study of the resources available to maintain development. I should like to see the Atlantic development board encouraging secondary industry in Nova Scotia in these direct ways, in the closest co-operation with the provincial government of that province.
I suppose there will be squabbles occasionally about to whom the political credit for these activities should be given. However,
[Mr. Stewart.)
I do not think the possibility of such squabbles, repulsive though they are, should deter us from taking this step if on other grounds it is desirable. We simply cannot afford to allow political pettiness to frustrate a program which is vital to the people of our region and, indirectly, to the entire nation to which the Atlantic area presents a special problem, as a result of its lack of economic development. I should hope that if this were acceptable to the province of Nova Scotia the board would seek authorization from this government to establish procedures allowing for direct co-operation with agencies of the province of Nova Scotia.
But even if our primary industries were flourishing and even if a score of new secondary industries were added, neither the prosperity nor the employment to which we aspire would result. A high division of labour in the provision of services as well as of goods is needed in Nova Scotia. Major population centres are needed, for it is only in such centres that a high proliferation of the service industries is possible. This means that new industrial developments should be planned and encouraged, not sporadically, but around natural or established centres, such as Hali-fax-Dartmouth, Mulgrave-Port Hawkesbury, and New Glasgow. Consequently, it would seem desirable to have Halifax-Dartmouth included just as soon as possible among the areas eligible for the various development incentives introduced by this government.
The necessary agencies for co-operation between the board and the various departments of the federal government are in existence. What is needed now is a vigorous and imaginative pooling of ideas and efforts between the Atlantic development board, the provincial government of Nova Scotia, the various municipalities and the various departments of this government.
So far, I have been inviting your attention, Mr. Speaker, to certain internal aspects of regional development in Atlantic Canada. I now wish to turn to the question of transportation, chiefly transportation between Atlantic Canada and the rest of the continent. It would be the height of folly to spend scores of millions of dollars encouraging secondary industry; it would be the height of folly to allow special tax incentives to new industries in this area, if those industries are to be choked off by transportation practices based on false notions masquerading as sound policy. We may assume that in the absence of some compelling reason, such as the location of natural resources, business in Canada will be drawn by savings in transportation and communication costs to the area roughly between Montreal and Windsor. This

does not mean we should forget our efforts to build up and maintain a transcontinental Canada any more than the difficulties imposed by the law of gravity mean we should not build and maintain houses. We must face this question of transportation and communication costs. If we are prepared to insist upon the result we must be prepared to pay the price. If we propose, as I assume we all do, to maintain a prosperous ocean-to-ocean economy, it is necessary for us to have something which we have not had recently or, perhaps, ever, namely a new and clearly enunciated transportation policy.
The "value of service" system of fixing freight rates, under which the value of the commodity to be carried is highly influential in determining the amount to be charged by the transportation company, permitted interregional subsidization in favour of the mari-times; but at the same time it encouraged maritime industry to concentrate on the supplying of raw materials rather than on the supplying of manufactured or processed goods. For this reason, among others, our small manufacturing industries, unable to compete on the larger Canadian market by reason of higher transportation costs, closed down; and here we are, three or four generations later, striving to repair that damage.
Moreover, between 1947 and the present we have ignored the unpleasant fact that we must pay the transportation costs of national existence. We have allowed the laws of transportation economics to hold greater and greater sway. As trucking competition grew in the central region of the country the railways were obliged to hold down freight rate increases there and to seek compensating revenues at the extremities of the country. Each permission to increase rates had a compounding effect at the extremities-what I like to call the "saucer" effect. The present situation is aptly described in the report of the MacPherson royal commission on transportation. At page 27 of the first volume the commissioners state:
These inequities-
They are referring to the inequities in the railway freight structure:
-are principally a result of the fact that the railways' competitive position relative to other carriers has declined and, as a consequence, they have been forced to obtain a greater relative share of the revenues they require from the traffic which is least affected by competition. And, since the position of the railways vis-a-vis their competitors seems to continue to decline with each passing year, the degree of inequity experienced by the traffic still tied to the rails continues to grow with each general increase in freight rates which the railways are permitted to apply. If such a process is allowed to continue the end results are dismal to contemplate: either railway rates will become so high that "captive" traffic cannot move
The Budget-Mr. Stewart at all or else competitors will inevitably arrive on the scene to relieve the "captives" from their bondage-in either case, a source of revenue upon
which the railways are increasingly dependant will have disappeared and the railway financial position will have become completely untenable.
In this situation you will understand readily why moves to keep the St. Lawrence river open longer and longer each year, and thus to bypass the Atlantic ports, seem calculated to heap insuit upon injury.
Hon. members must realize that transportation policies are as vitally important to the future of the Atlantic provinces now as they have ever been in the years of our confederation. In 1867 the prospect of plunging Nova Scotia into the bedevilled cauldron of Upper and Lower Canadian politics was far from enticing. We were able to accept the invitation because it was clearly understood that national policy, especially national policy on transportation, would make confederation economically viable for us. We have no desire to become an 18th century-style mercantile colony, a colony preserved as a market for Ontario and Quebec while at the same time developments in transportation promote, first, the shipment out of the province of raw materials rather than finished goods and, second, the bypassing of our ports.
We still have no desire to become an 18th century-style mercantile colony.
We applaud the decision of this government to look into the ways in which the ports of Saint John and Halifax can be modernized. We regard that as a good harbinger of the future.
We know that efforts are being made to bring tourists into the Atlantic provinces by developing attractions there, such as the great fortress at Louisburg and the establishment of a new national park in the western part of Nova Scotia. Efforts are being made in various ways to encourage manufacturing there. Obviously additional provision is now needed for rapid and ample transportation facilities for both tourists and trucks between western Nova Scotia and new England. This is one specific thing that should be done immediately. But, sir, we are hoping for more from this government.
Since 1927 the government of Canada has been paying the railways millions of dollars each year in an effort to discharge the obligations to the maritime provinces recognized by the Duncan royal commission and by the preamble to the Maritime Freight Rates Act. Surely, now that the railways have lost the monopolistic position they formerly enjoyed in many parts of the country, things are ripe for us to ascertain if these annual payments to the railways offer the way most beneficial to the maritime provinces for the discharge

The Budget-Mr. Stewart ot these obligations. These payments have been established in a statutory way and their validity is beyond doubt. What is not certain is that these payments should be paid directly to the railways, thus running the risk that they become a subsidy to the railways, rather than assistance to the shippers in the Atlantic provinces.
The present government already has begun to pay 90 per cent of the cost of completing the trans-Canada highway. I urge the government to remember its commitment, and here I quote directly from the pamphlet entitled, "A better break for the Atlantic provinces", to make available "financial assistance for building trunk highways in all four provinces to promote the tourist industry and provide better access to resources and markets". I think this is a commitment the discharge of which this government should undertake very soon; in fact, a beginning should be made this year. It would perhaps be a small beginning, but at least it would be a beginning.
In addition, I should like to see the government examine most seriously the possibility of obtaining permission from the appropriate United States authorities for the construction of an all-weather highway across the state of Maine to connect the Atlantic provinces with the eastern townships of Quebec, Montreal, and Ontario. The distance from Montreal to Moncton is, after all, only 400 miles; and the benefits from such a highway would be obvious. But there is a benefit which is not immediately obvious, and it is that it would introduce into the transportation situation in the Atlantic provinces a degree of competition such as is highly recommended by the MacPherson royal commission on transportation. I am not saying that this is something which inevitably should be done; I am saying that in this situation, where we need to review our transportation policy, it is something which should be considered and examined rapidly and thoroughly.
If unemployment is the major economic problem of the country, and if this has become a regional problem, then sir, the matters I have been putting before the house are of great concern. In 1867 Canada was joined by Nova Scotia very reluctantly, but we have overcome our reluctance and are now determined to do all we can to make Canada succeed economically, culturally and politically for the people of all its provinces. Our own economy is developing quite well. We are anxious to have it develop even better so that as the years go on we can make a greater and greater contribution to what we hope over the years will be a more and more perfect union.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart) and followed some of his remarks very carefully. In particular he referred to criticisms which had been made of the Liberal program, I imagine referring to members of the opposition, and described them as a red herring. Let me say at once that there were none who paraded before the country in the last campaign more consistently than the Liberal party, criticizing the previous government's financial administration. At this stage of the game, viewed in retrospect, and in view of what has transpired, this is regrettable, because now we find greater areas of spending. Although the deficit appears to have reduced, we find in actual fact it would not have been, if the payment of corporation tax had not been moved forward. But for that I venture to say the deficit would have been equally as great in the coming year as it ever was in the past, perhaps even greater.
However, the point I wish to make initially is not that, but rather to indicate the confusion which exists as a result of government policy since the Liberal party took office a year ago this month. I think the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) put his finger on the point this afternoon when, in answer to a question regarding the filing of applications for social security, he said there had been some confusion. He may not have actually used that word; he may have said "misunderstanding"; but this confusion has spread into three or four fields, such as into the teaching profession, into crown corporations, and so on. The present government are currently known more for this than or anything else. Let me say that the program of confusion which has existed since the government took office in April of last year is one which needs a little further investigation at this time, and I am glad to have this opportunity to bring these matters to the attention of the government, and particularly to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon).
I should like to begin by giving the house a list of those areas in which I believe the government has mismanaged the affairs of the country, where they have caused confusion. In actual fact, in an age when we should be considering where the country as a whole is going it seems to me the government is unable to lift us, to give us leadership, or to give us direction in any of these fields.
First of all may I point to the present commission on bilingualism and bicultural-ism. With that I would couple the attitude
(Mr. Stewart.]

currently taken by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Next is the situation which is being created in this country by this government owing to their proposed Canada pension plan. The third area, Mr. Speaker, concerns the redistribution of electoral boundaries. Another is government policy regarding veterans hospitals. Another is the situation regarding the flag we presently have for Canada. A further one concerns agricultural policy and the problems which exist within the country. Then there is the situation in the Department of Labour itself, which the government has brought about through its handling of the current dispute with the S.I.U. Another one concerns defence policy. For a government which has acted in the way it has and has spoken in the past in the way it has, the present policy of the government, although it may be desirable from the public's point of view, in restropect is a peculiar attitude for the government to take. Another area concerns unemployment insurance, and what has happened in this house during the past two weeks, to which I will be making further reference. Then recently there was the federal-provincial conference, and I draw attention to the relations which have existed since that time.
No doubt many hon. members in the house, even on the government side, could give me a longer list than the one I have just spelled out, Mr. Speaker, but I think that is enough for one contributor to this debate. To begin with-and again I refer to the transportation policies which were discussed by the previous speaker-I should like to make reference to something which was not in my mind previous to hearing the hon. member. I refer to the discussions which have taken place between the government and the industry which is most common in my constituency, the furniture industry. For the benefit of the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Moreau) we would probably be referred to as a rural constituency by most hon. members in this house. However, in the constituency of Grey-Bruce we have the largest centre for the manufacture of hard furniture in the Dominion of Canada. I know the government is thinking in terms of a reduction in tariffs in this field. This is an industry which is indigenous to the area in which it is currently located, and it would mean an end to that industry in Canada if this reduction took place. As a result of the situation which existed prior to the present government taking over the treasury benches, the people employed in that industry know only too well where their prosperity came from.
Before I proceed may I make a brief reference to some of the words used by the
The Budget-Mr. Winkler Minister of Finance at the time of the introduction of his budget. He said, as reported at page 969 of Hansard:
All hon. members can take satisfaction from the improvement that has been occurring in economic conditions in Canada and from the optimism with which we can view the immediate future.
Those words would be true, Mr. Speaker, had he told us from whence and from what policies this outlook had emanated. It certainly did not result from anything which he presented to this house.
When I look back, Mr. Speaker, at his first budget and compare it with the one he has just brought down, it would seem that in 1963 he was trying to play the bad boy in the ball park and was saying: "If you won't let me bat I won't play". Then after he saw what could be done by his playmates in the field he threw his bat away and went home anyway. He has thrown out every policy he intended to bring into the house, except for one or two, such as the imposition of sales tax on building materials; and it would have been a lot better for him had he thrown that one out as well. Then this year, 1964, the Minister of Finance came in looking as though he had the world in his hands and made a very lengthy budget speech with what seemed a full bag that evening; but when the evening was over there was nothing there. It was full of hot air, and I think the country received it in exactly the same fashion. We are now in the second year of Liberal administration and all we find is the addition of confusion, to which I made initial reference in opening my remarks.
I also think of the introduction of his budget this year, which leads me to believe from my knowledge of the circumstances that this is the complete and total cause for the situation which has existed in this house over the last two weeks. As I said before, I shall be making further reference to this matter in due course.
If I may quote again from the remarks of the Minister of Finance in introducing his budget this year, he continued with these words:
The deficit in our current account balance of payments with other countries is still too large but it is smaller than it has been since 1954. The prospects for the current year are good;
Then later he said this:
Employment, production and incomes should all be substantially higher than last year for the country as a whole.
Then further:
It was necessary to move quickly on a number of fronts, and understandably some of the proposals that were put forward were questioned at the time.

The Budget

Mr. Winkler
I would say that almost every proposal that was put forward was questioned at that time. Then he went on:
It is now clear, however, that the main policy changes proposed last spring and summer have paid off well and will continue to pay off in the months and years ahead.
I do not know that the Minister of Finance at any time ever gave credit to the previous administration. He may have, but certainly in the tenor of his address to the house that evening he indicated to the country that any progress made was due to the policies which he and his government brought forward. Nothing could be further from the truth.
All that the Liberal representatives, who were sent to my constituency prior to the last election campaign, complained about was the financial problems we had in the country. In contrast, I wonder what the Minister of Finance and his colleagues would say this year. We have been assured that there is not going to be an election this year, and that is news after the interesting things which have transpired during the last few days. In fact I noticed a very large number of prominent persons of the Liberal party in town today, and they did not know themselves why they were here. That in itself may not mean anything, but it indicates what was suggested as having transpired last week may have been true.
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, representatives of the minister's party came into my constituency during the 1963 campaign, and prior to it, criticizing me and the administration I represented for its financial and agricultural policies. I doubt if they would go back to my constituency today and say the same things because the results of their policies are too well known.
Some hon. members opposite speak of "this government" and "that government". I still say this is our government, and nothing has been done by our government in 1964 for the agricultural industry in central Canada. Nothing has been done for the province of Ontario.
What happened to commodity prices after the 1963 April election? Ask the farmers. They know what transpired. With regard to deficit financing, it is well known that the previous administration would not have had budget deficit in some periods had it not given increased grants to the provinces. But that is not the way the Liberals painted the picture for the people. Their deportment was one of conceit, which is a regrettable thing when they propose a program to the people of Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Political fraud.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, political fraud. Dealing with what transpired in the house during the last two weeks it is certainly peculiar that the government, and in certain instances much of the press, were very critical of the way we acted. I have here two motions which I might quote, but for the sake of brevity I will not. They deal with the same question of unemployment insurance and show that the former administration acted reasonably in looking after the situation. Nothing like what happened last week would or did occur at the time the Conservative party, under its present leader, formed the government.
The people are well aware of this. They are well aware where the blame lies for what happened in the last few weeks, and there is one very interesting observation that I would like to quote:
I suppose this is neither the time nor the place to discuss the reasons for what I might call the mess in which the whole of parliament is at the present time. Whether it is due to the intellectual or political amateurism of one. or the stupid obstinacy of the other, or the blatant opportunism of any other party.
Maybe the rules of debate do not permit us to read speeches made in the other place, but that statement was made in the other place by a supporter of the party that forms the government. What happened in the last two weeks was a shame, and a mark on the parliament of Canada. It showed the inability of the present government to manage its own affairs.
One can quote all sorts of editorials to support the view that I am taking, but in fact I place the blame on the Minister of Finance. I believe he wanted his budget hurriedly dealt with, before he went to the conference in Quebec city, so that there he could say there was nothing more to be discussed in that regard. All that remained then would have been the Canada pension plan. He could have told the provinces the federal government could not make a greater contribution to their needs, and that would have been the end of that.
But realizing at the end of the fourth day of the budget debate that there was no time to finish it and get the other business through before Easter, the Minister of Finance acceded to the wishes of others in his party and we went on to deal with interim supply and the supplementary estimates. At this stage I do not think it is necessary for me to quote the Prime Minister, but we took him at his word when he outlined the business that had to be done before the Easter recess.
On April 1 I put a question to the Minister of Labour, which he finally answered, saying that he was aware of the crisis in the unemployment insurance fund prior to the Easter

week end. I am not making any of these comments just to say I wanted to have Easter week off, because I was one of those who were here during the course of that week. On April 3 I asked the Minister of Finance if he was aware of the crisis in the fund, and after some lecturing he said he was also.
Since that time the Minister of Labour has seen fit to lecture us on what should and should not be our duties. He took a very arrogant Liberal party view of our duties and said it was our duty to look for this information, suggesting we were delinquent in our homework by not getting the information which we sought from him. The attitude of the Minister of Finance was exactly the same. Obviously, therefore, the whole crisis that existed was due to the introduction of the budget and the failure of the government to realize the seriousness of the situation. The government could have borrowed the money for the fund up until midnight of the Tuesday of the following week, but it did not see fit to do so after it felt it had the opposition in a position of prejudice and that it could arrogantly force its views on them.
We would have failed in our basic duty to the people of Canada if we had acquiesced in the desire of the treasury benches at that time. We did not then, and we never will, particularly if they try to crowd us into accepting these things. How else could we have found out the seriousness of the situation with regard to the unemployment insurance fund? Any blame for that situation must be placed on the shoulders of those occupying the treasury benches.
I have one editorial here from the Winnipeg Free Press, a newspaper that is not always, if ever, too friendly to the party on this side of the house, and the editorial is in support of the statement made by the hon. gentleman in the other place. Whether it was right or wrong let us not try to pull any nonsense in this house by saying it was the responsibility of the opposition. It is a very sorry thing when supporters of the Liberal party go around, trying to create the impression among the people of Canada that we have spent a long time on the supplementary estimates when they, while in opposition, spent a total of 26J days on supplementary estimates, eight of them devoted to the Department of Labour.
With regard to the budget, the point that is most often brought to my attention when I visit my constituency is the adamant view of the Minister of Finance in continuing and increasing the sales tax on building materials. Because of this tax the farmer is caught in a squeeze from which he cannot escape. Even in the case of minor repairs he has to pay this
The Budget-Mr. Winkler tax, and this despite the fact that his monetary return from the commodities he produces is so low.
Again I return to one of the points I mentioned, namely defence policy. I cannot deny that there is a measure of agreement throughout the country in regard to some of the ideas being proposed. We must not always look back, Mr. Speaker; there is no question but that we have to look forward. However, in retrospect I find it a most peculiar thing that the Liberal party should use the tactics it did with the armed services during the last election campaign and then turn around and introduce the policy it has now introduced.
The Prime Minister has said that the Liberals are not interested in going to the country. He knows full well that the reason lies in the results of the policies they have introduced. As I go down the list of items it is a list of total confusion and badly prepared legislation so far as Canada is concerned.
I should like to deal with a point with regard to which I believe the government can take immediate action, to repair some of the damage that has been done. I refer to their so-called efforts in the field of bicul-turalism, and I make these remarks without any reference whatsoever to our friends and fellow citizens in the province of Quebec. I have in my hand an article from the Winnipeg Tribune of Saturday, April 4, 1964, dealing with a speech made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet) to his constituents, I imagine. He had this to say in western Canada:
If Quebec leaves confederation western Canada will be forced to its knees, begging for help and aid from Washington.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what degree of unity is there in words like those uttered by a minister of the government on the treasury benches? What can they expect? They say to us that we have to make greater efforts. Who is causing the dissension? Who is causing the situation that exists? It is my humble opinion that if the commission at present touring the country had never been formed the confusion that exists today would not have occurred.
I believe too that when the government thinks over things that have happened in the past they must have some soul searching moments when they wonder what on earth they have created in this parliament. I am referring now, Mr. Speaker, to the present situation in regard to the Canada pension plan and what has transpired. I believe that the pressure that has been exerted by the government on the province of Ontario is

The Budget-Mr. Winkler most unfair. It seems to me that the premier of Ontario has now made a study of the entire situation. He has voiced his opinions on several occasions and he now seems to favour the plan that has been outlined in the province of Quebec, an outline that I have here. But first, Mr. Speaker, let me refer to some words taken from the report of the 1950 joint committee on old age security. I find the following on page 107 of that report:
The committee further believes that such a program-
A social security program.
-can be financed and administered satisfactorily only by the federal government. Only the federal authority can establish a sufficiently broad base of contributions to make such a program possible, and only the federal authorities can ensure that an individual will receive the benefit to which he has contributed, regardless of whether he moves from one province to another.
It is a peculiar situation, Mr. Speaker, when we examine what has taken place up to the present time. I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette which quotes the premier of the province of Quebec as saying that there is "no possibility" of Quebec entering the national plan. The articles goes on to say that Mr. Lesage was adamant in his position with regard to the federal project.
If that is the case today, what has caused the change of heart? The reason must be nothing more than sheer politics. The government likes to accuse us of introducing politics into the house from time to time, but you can see that they are at it almost all the time. Even back as far as 1950 they started to play politics with this matter and if I had been able to do more research and examine the records further I am sure I would have found other instances.
That being the case, I find the situation most peculiar when I look back to 1957 when the change of government took place, and when I refer to the attacks that were made on the leadership of the party that formed the government then. It is a peculiar thing how all this has taken place. There were names then that were important in this particular field such as Laporte, Levesque and Laurendeau. Those names were known then, as well as the attitudes they adopted and the positions they took. But now that they are in hallowed places we must not say anything. We cannot say anything about this matter. But I say to hon. members that if the Quebec Liberals want to adopt a certain attitude in the province of Quebec and to segregate themselves from the Liberal party nationally I do not blame them. It is a strange thing that the Prime Minister cannot maintain any degree of cohesion or unity within his own party at the


federal level; and if he cannot do that, how does he think he can maintain cohesion and unity throughout the nation? I do not know how it can be done. It is a very peculiar situation.
This is not the only incident. From 1957 on there were all sorts of other incidents in which the party across the floor was most efficient in attacking people's characters.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member not agree that, no matter what happens, so far as the pension plan is concerned it was this government's initiative that forced Premier Robarts into a public plan?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the sort of statement we can expect from one who cannot cash a government cheque in his own constituency. That is all I have to say. As a matter of fact, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) is spending money as though it was going out of style I would be ashamed to stand up in the House of Commons and say I cannot cash a cheque in my own constituency. Certainly the Minister of Finance has got more than he needs and I believe he might have ripped up the cheque and given the hon. member the money anyway. However, that is behind us.
The suggestion I wish to make at this point is simply this. I do not believe for one minute what was said by the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Moreau), because in the discussion on redistribution I think he showed he did not have a clear understanding of what the situation is in Canada. He talked about rural tyranny. Let me tell you this, Mr. Speaker. If the government places the tolerance figure at less than 33J per cent it will add to the confusion with regard to the things I have mentioned this afternoon and cause more confusion in the country and, no matter when the Prime Minister calls the election, they will not be in office after it is over. Of that I am very sure.
Because the hon. member has referred to the premier of Ontario I am going to say this in concluding my remarks. It seems to me that a more thorough study has been made in other quarters than has been made by the federal government with regard to pensions for Canadians. What about the farmers? The farmers are concerned; they are turning against the government because not only do they not understand the situation but they are coming to believe it is going to cost them more for less. There are so many people who will not be covered by the federal plan that many people who have plans of their own

in industrial plants want no part of the federal plan. This is the truth, Mr. Speaker. I am not deceiving anyone.
Our position is clear. The former minister of national health and welfare has made it clear. We want a plan and are going to support a plan but we do not think this plan is good enough. Mr. Lesage has brought forth a plan that is clear. I have it right here. There are survivor benefits, disability benefits and many other benefits plus a higher cash return, although the premium may be a little larger.
It has been proven actuarially that the premium will be higher also for the federal plan. I believe that if the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the government want to do one thing, and do it immediately and quickly, to cause some degree of unity in Canada, they should consider reconvening the provincial premiers conference, study Mr. Lesage's plan and adopt it. Then they could invite these provinces to join us in a plan that will be at least national in scope.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to take advantage of the latitude afforded in this debate to raise briefly two subjects which are not directly related to the budget introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). My first observation, Mr. Speaker, is that I dissent vigorously from the remarks made in this chamber last Friday by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). I am sorry he is not here. I have told him that I propose to discuss his remarks, but apparently he cannot be here at the moment. He said, during the debate on Friday, that the remainder of Canada should give up trying to meet what he described as the insatiable demands of Quebec and should proceed on the assumption that Canada will consist of nine provinces. The hon. member in these remarks spoke for himself. I have no doubt he will find some people who will agree with him but I, for one, wish to repudiate such a defeatist view.
I believe, and I think there are many others who are not French Canadians who will continue to believe that we should give serious and sympathetic consideration to the genuine grievances of French Canada within confederation. I believe also, and I think there are many French Canadians who will agree with me on this, that concessions to provincial demands, from whatever source they come, should not go so far as to destroy the power of the federal government to give effective leadership in matters affecting Canada as a whole. I cite for example such things as full employment, opportunity for economic growth across Canada, and so on.
The Budget-Mr. Brewin We know that reconciliation of these two conflicting aims may not be easy, but it must be achieved.
I do not believe that with the present difficulties of confederation, observations such as those made by the hon. member for Skeena are helpful, however sincere they may be, or however much they may reflect some existing attitudes throughout Canada. In my view the members of all parties, from wherever they come in Canada, have a duty to interpret to the people of our country the spirit of compromise and conciliation upon which Canada was built. This spirit is still necessary today if Canada is going forward as a genuine partnership between the two founding nations. I believe we have a duty of interpretation to those Canadians who are neither French speaking nor English speaking, and who sometimes find it difficult to understand the historic realities upon which Canada was built.

Mr. Speaker, I thought I would underscore these few words by repeating them in French. But my knowledge of French is limited. I know that my French colleagues understand me very well when I speak English, so I will refrain. However, I would like to reassure them, and those whom they represent of the sincerity and the good faith, of the majority of the Canadian people, and of their determination to do everything in their power to understand and satisfy their grievances.

My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), asks what contribution my French is to the unity of Canada. All I can say is, at least it is an effort.
I should like now to say something about this parliament. I believe there is a general impression that parliament is floundering, and such an impression does harm to every party represented here and to parliamentary-democracy itself. I believe the situation is urgent. Some of the difficulties are those of procedure and I hope that the special committee, under your chairmanship, sir, will be able soon to recommend some radical and effective changes. In the meantime I suggest that the Prime Minister and leaders of the other parties should get together and evolve a plan for the early and effective dispatch of the business of this house before the summer recess.
This suggestion is by no means original. I noticed it, for example, in the columns of my hon. friend, the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). If some temporary alteration of the rules is necessary, and could
2100	HOUSE OF
Suggested House Proceedings Broadcast be made, as I believe it could, without interfering with the basic rights of members, then I think the house would be willing to give favourable consideration to it.
It looks to me, Mr. Speaker, as though it is getting close to five o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It being five o'clock, the house will now proceed to a consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely notices of motions.

That a special committee of the house be appointed to consider and make recommendations on a system of televising and radio broadcasting of the proceedings or part of the proceedings of this house.
He said: It was by chance, Mr. Speaker, and not by design that I find myself addressing the house, as it were, in sections or in instalments and on different subjects. The motion before the house, which I am bringing forward, provides for the appointment of a special committee to make recommendations on a system for televising and radio broadcasting of the proceedings or part of the proceedings of this house. The purpose of this suggestion is to improve the procedure of the house and also to use the best means of bringing to the public the proceedings in the house.
Parliament has been described as the paramount forum of the nation. I suggest that all interested citizens should have an opportunity to see and to hear what is done in their name by their representatives. I further suggest that television and radio are the best means of carrying out this objective. This house is not a private club or debating society. This is the forum in which the great issues affecting the country are discussed, or at least should be discussed by the men and women elected to do so. The original meaning of the word "forum" was "marketplace". Who would suggest that a marketplace should not be as open to the public as possible?
There has been a tendency, Mr. Speaker, in recent days to deride parliament. Just about a year ago Mr. Charles Pannell, member for Leeds West in the British House of Commons, pointed out: "It is not a new fashion to deride parliament. It has all been done before, and done better". During one of his speeches, Mr. Pannell gave some illustrations of his point. On August 4, 1661, Mr. Pepys, in his diary, recorded how an acquaintance said to him:


How basely things have been carried on in parliament by the young men that did labour to oppose all things that were moved by serious men -that they are the most profane, swearing fellows that ever he heard in his life, which makes him think they will spoil all and bring things into a war again if they can.
Charles Dickens, the well known writer and observer in the press gallery-I probably do not need to explain who he is-decried parliament in these words:
The great dust heap of Westminster.. .laughing, coughing, oh-ing, groaning, a conglomeration of noise and confusion to be met with in no other place in existence, not excepting Smithfield on a market day or a cockpit in all its glory.
In 1830, the essayist Hazlitt wrote this:
Talk of mobs. See how few who have distinguished themselves in the House of Commons have ever done anything else.
Robert Louis Stevenson said: "We all know what parliament is and we are ashamed of it." And Carlyle asked:
How is it possible to believe, much less to think, that in the Commons is rooted the strength of England, and not its weakness?
At the present time in Britain a group of Conservatives are circulating a paper under the ominous title, "Change or Decay". As Mr. Pannell said, it is a sort of legend that parliament has been a noble institution which has fallen into decay. Nevertheless, in his view, parliament today is more sober than ever it was. Generally, he says, we are not lesser men than our grandfathers were.
I do not know whether these encouraging words, which are applied to the United Kingdom House of Commons, the mother of parliaments, are equally applicable to the Canadian parliament, but I do suggest that much of the deploring being done about the Canadian parliament today is vastly exaggerated. However, this is not a ground for complacency and whatever can be done to improve parliament and bring it closer to the people, should be done. I expressed earlier, in another context, the hope that the special committee will report at an early date, and that its report will be vigorous and radical with regard to what needs to be done to improve parliament.
The suggestion I make in this resolution is one of a number of reforms which could be achieved. I do not suggest for a moment that it is the most urgent, but I think it should be considered by the special committee. I suggest that the televising and radio broadcasting of the sessions of this house would have beneficial effects both on the conduct of debate and, if I may use an over-worked expression, upon the image of parliament. Nor should hon. members be frightened by the novelty of my suggestion. There are always "stick-in-the-muds" who object to

anything new, and quite a few of them seem to find their way into various parliaments. Proposals similar to mine are being discussed at the present time in the British House of Commons. I should like to refer to the views on this matter of three of its members, one from each of the three historic parties in Britain. First, I should like to quote Mr. Iain Macleod, speaking in a debate on parliamentary reform on March 15, 1963. Mr. Macleod was at that time leader of the house, although I think he has since fallen into some disgrace with the Conservative party after having objected to the mysterious processes by which the present prime minister was chosen. Mr. Macleod, speaking of the proposal to televise sessions of the house, said:
I do not think we should be too afraid of this. I remember very well two instances, one of enormous importance and one of much less importance. where I believe that before the event people were afraid of the impact of television. The one of the greatest importance of all was the coronation of Her Majesty the Queen. Many people were deeply worried and desperately anxious about it and thought that it was wrong that television cameras should go into Westminster abbey. In fact it was one of the finest programs that has ever been put on and one of the greatest services that could possibly have been given to the royal family. The other incident I have in mind was a question about which very many people were worried-the televising of party conferences. Many people thought that we should all end up speaking exclusively to the television cameras. As we know, this does not happen.
When a Mr. Curran intervened to suggest there would be certain mechanical difficulties, Mr. Macleod replied:
I am certain that these arguments are formidable, but they are also not insuperable.
The next objection, raised by a Mrs. Judith Hart, was that the selectivity which would result from an edited version of proceedings in the house would do damage to the quality of speeches. Mr. Macleod replied:
It is possible, but one has exactly this difficulty with the sort of programs that exist already and which inevitably compress the events, as in the newspapers and on sound radio.
Perhaps I may turn now to the observations of Mr. Grimmond, the leader of the Liberal party in Great Britain-I hope that by referring to him I will secure some support from hon. members opposite. In the same debate, he said this:
The press, the B.B.C. and television keep democracy ticking over and once the press ceases to report the House of Commons, democracy will suffer. Every day the main headlines in the press are about things raised in the House of Commons and, much as we complain about the press, and I do, do not let us delude ourselves, the press is a vital part of democracy and this is one reason why I have changed my views on television. I used to be against the idea of televising the House

That is the real point of what I am saying. But perhaps the most vigorous exponent of television in the British House of Commons is Mr. Anthony Wedgwood Benn of the Labour party. Mr. Benn, as most of the members of this house know, was a distinguished commoner who inherited a title and was subsequently the subject matter, one might say, of legislation which enabled him to step down from the House of Peers and revert to the rank of commoner. In this he blazed a path for the present Prime Minister, Sir Alec Home-is it pronounced "Hume"? I am not sure.
As reported in the Manchester Guardian of March 21, 1963, Mr. Benn has this to say:
The time has now come to launch a campaign to televise the House of Commons. For how much longer are we going to have to put up with getting our parliamentary reporting by courtesy of the popular press and the self appointed television commentators? Why can't the cameras come to Westminster and show us as we are?
The House of Commons is the grand forum of the nation or nothing at all. Here, government policies must be deployed and criticised; here, the opposition must reveal and defend its alternative in broad outline; here, those who exercise power must be held accountable for the use they make of it to backbenchers of all parties; here the quality of men and women is continuously assessed by colleagues who know them intimately and who see how they react to stress and defeat as well as how they take their moments of glory.
The M.P.s who carry weight and are respected for their knowledge and integrity are not by any means always the same ones as those who shine in the contrived four-minute knockabout beloved by the television producers.
If the House of Commons let in the cameras, people would see us, warts and all. They might not like us all the time, but parliamentary debate is a substitute for civil war and they would more likely share our moments of passion than mock us for showing them. At any rate, they would be judging us by what we are and not what others, for their own purposes want to make us out to be.
Why, then, is the Commons not televised? Because many members-and this is more a matter of age than political affiliation-fear some loss of dignity and intimacy, and visualize nightmarish arc lights and even make-up and the heady atmosphere of party conferences. In truth the cameras would soon be forgotten once they were installed. Few younger M.P.s on all sides are impressed by these objections and for them the television lens holds out no more horror-or promise-than the sight of a journalist, pencil in hand, at a political meeting.
Televising parliament will, of course, come in time. The question really is, why not now, when it could do some real good? If there is to be a break-through it has got to be made an issue and not discussed interminably.
I heartily endorse the words of Mr. Benn and commend them to the members of this house. Of course there are objections. Some of them have already been mentioned and disposed of in the quotation from what Mr. 2102	HOUSE OF
