I had occasion to discuss this matter of television with the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who raised, amongst other objections, the fact that members would, as he put it, "posture" when they were on television in the house. I cannot see the force of this objection. Is it not the essence of being part of a public forum that we are required to posture to some extent? Surely we cannot expect in this public forum to have the pleasantness of privacy as in a club, where we can snooze comfortably or chat intimately with our friends. It may be objected that some of our member are more photogenic than others. This is, of course, inevitable, but I cannot think that most of the members of this house need have any misgivings on this score. Each of us no doubt has his own individual type of charm which at least some of our friends and constituents will appreciate if they see us on television. I do not forget, and I remind the house, that the downfall of Senator Joe McCarthy was credited to television, as was the election of the late President Kennedy. I hope I will not be thought to be interfering in any way with or making improper remarks about the politics of another country, but I think those events can be credited to television, and I think they were all to the good.
All in all, it is my guess that if we were televised we would tend to behave a little better, rather than a little worse, if we knew that we might find ourselves revealed, warts and all, to the candid camera, reproducing our contributions to parliament in the private homes of people across Canada.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the televising of parliament would be a contribution to Canadian unity. Instead of centring their attention upon local heroes, the people of Canada would have the opportunity to get to know the great men of other provinces and regions; we would perhaps be able to develop a sense that parliament spoke for all the people of Canada, instead of being merely the exponent of local and regional problems. I admit that there are technical problems and that the experiment would certainly not be successful if undue selectivity meant that a special show was put on by a few chosen individuals at the time selected for television. But surely, if the opportunity is provided, these objections can be dealt with. Nothing would ever be done and no change ever made if we were to concentrate our minds on the objections alone. Mr. Speaker, I conclude by asking the house to take this motion seriously. I think by adopting it- it cannot come about right away-it would contribute to that much needed development, 

the interest of the people of Canada in parliament, and the renewal of the basic function of parliament as the grand forum of the nation.

Mr. Speaker, to follow up the explanations the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) has just given about his motion and to which I listened very attentively not to say religiously, I must tell you very sincerely that, since I read that motion, I have been both amused and interested by that suggestion, and you can no doubt guess why.
I had already noticed-with all the sense of humour I can muster and the few notions I have in this field-that, curiously enough, whereas I personally put an end to almost 16 years of work in radio, television and journalism to devote myself actively to politics, a few hon. members in this house, on the contrary, took advantage of their entrance into active politics to become on a regular basis, journalists, radio commentators and television moderators.
I have no wish to discuss here their personal merit, their success or lack of success, far from it, because I know from experience that they have assumed a very hard job, a very heavy task, considering all the work required of a responsible member of this house who must above all have that important qualification of attendance with regard to the sittings of the house, and the committees, not to mention his own personal work, in order to give his constituents a good and fair representation.
Now the hon. member for Greenwood- no doubt, in order to facilitate and reconcile those twofold responsibilities-seems to suggest an agreeable and practical way of discharging those responsibilities, by enabling hon. members to do all that without leaving the house. It is a gallant gesture with regard to all of us, I admit, but I seriously wonder whether introducing such a system of radio or T.V. broadcasting of part of our proceedings would really help "equally" all hon. members and bring about anything really desirable for the Canadian people.
When I refer to some of our sittings, you will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, that the true and earnest spirit of hard work which should prevail in our proceedings would be seriously questioned, and rightly so, by the listeners or viewers. Of course, this might be a good thing, if we were sure it would bring a marked improvement in our proceedings and the quality of our discussions, but it must be admitted that it would take a bold man to say so.

Several factors play a part in radio programs, and still more in television programs. For instance, the tone of voice, the delivery of the speech, the quality and correctness of the language, the right clothes, the posture or the poise of the participant, his better profile and also, Mr. Speaker, and not the the least, the "gesture" which is most important on television.
You may be sure, Mr. Speaker, that we would certainly get our money's worth just watching the gestures which the hon. members of this house would be making on television. There we would have bellicose gestures which might serve the cause of separatism, or gestures worthy of the top-ranking heroes in westerns, when they start pitching lead all over the place, or the eloquent, grandiose gestures of the great Shakespearian or Racinian actors of yore, not to mention in some cases the frantic arm-waving, Allegro con vivace, remindful of that grand maestro, Leopold Stokowski, leading his musicians in Richard Wagner's Die Walkure.
See where that might lead us. Considering those remarks, Mr. Speaker, you can anticipate all the sittings and rehearsals we would be compelled to make in order to give Canadian views a dignified and commendable show.
Then there would be all the people looking after management, lighting, props, make-up, and all those technicians in charge of sound or picture, to name but a few. However, there is in all that a practical aspect which I ought to mention: it would be a great step forward in fighting unemployment, by doubling the staff of the companies which would be in charge of these gigantic productions. Unfortunately our Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) who is not here, but who has so much to do, would certainly not be pleased with this new financial charge added to his budget already so heavily burdened.
In my opinion, however, there are more serious reasons not to pass such a measure, at least for the time being.
Many people, including myself, are of the opinion that our Canadian television is sick at the present time. The diagnoses of experts in this field are coming to us from all over Canada, so much so that several fact-finding committees are now being set up.
There are newspaper reports to that effect, as shown by these excerpts from Le Droit of Ottawa, for April 7:
A special committee on broadcasting is to be set up soon in Ottawa.
Indeed the Secretary of State (Mr. La-montagne) stated:
-that the federal government proposes to appoint a special committee on broadcasting in order to put an end to uncertainties in this field in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, just a few words to congratulate the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) for having introduced this motion.
I believe it would be worthwhile to form a committee of the house to see if it would be possible to try an experiment, first with radio, and then, later on, with television.
I believe there is no point in concealing things; we are elected by the people and we should not be ashamed to broadcast the proceedings of the house on radio or television.
I think it would be in the public interest, Mr. Speaker, since the public could see the behaviour of the members in the house and hear the answers given by the government when members of the opposition, or even government members, ask questions, and it could also find out about the attendance of the members, especially when a vote is taken.
It seems to me it would be important that the Canadian people learn, through radio and television, which members are present in the house or absent from it, which are those who take part in the debates and those who do not.
In my opinion, it would be in the public interest that all this be made known.
I appreciated the statements from the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Berger). By the way, I may say his constituents would have liked to see him on television, had this sitting been televised, because he had the proper gesture, the proper voice, everything. If only for the sole purpose of compelling members of the House of Commons who are paid $18,000 per year to attend the sittings of the house, I believe that the motion of the hon. member would be most useful not only to the Canadian people but also to the members themselves. Thanks to these media of direct communication, radio and television, the people would then be in a position to decide at election time, whether or not the absentee member should be returned to the house. Or this would prompt


members to resign automatically and to abstain from running for office in the next election, to be replaced by some active member who would always be present in the House of Commons to look after the interest of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, the proposal put forward today by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) is an interesting one in many respects. I should like to congratulate him for raising nearly every one of the objections which I had to televising part of the proceedings of this house and for giving his opinion as to how to deal with these objections.
X agree that there is a great need for a better appreciation of the activities of parliament by the general public of Canada. I say that because we have seen consistently reports in the press, which have to do their job in the best way they see fit, dealing for example, with want of confidence motions, in which reports certain members are accused of voting against the terms of the motion, whether it concerns sales tax, family allowances, medicare, or what-have-you, when the members concerned and even the mover of the want of confidence motion know very well that the only result which would eventuate from support of the motion would be to dissolve parliament.
That is just one example, but there are other matters which go on on parliament hill involving the activities of members of which the general public understand very little. For example, a lot has been said about attendance of members in this house. I think it is incorrect to presume that the members who spend the greatest number of hours sitting in their seats in this house are in fact doing the best jobs for their constituencies and for Canada.
I say that because, for example, all hon. members of the house specialize in one field or another. They may specialize in more than one department, but they certainly do not try to become experts in the whole spectrum of federal government administration. If my speciality happened to be agriculture, fisheries or forestry, and if I spent my whole time sitting in the house and did not prepare myself for the debates on these subjects, I could not really make a very valuable contribution to them.
As I said, there is a great need for the people to be better informed. But I am not sure whether this can be done by televising some of the proceedings of the house-although I have no objection to the setting up of a committee to look into the matter, and to see if it would be possible to do it on a trial basis. However, we will immediately

run into the problem of how much of the proceedings should be televised. In this connection, if it reaches that stage, I suggest the question period so that there would be a larger number of performers at any given time.
Do you think it is a good idea to have performers?

That is exactly what it is going to turn out to be. People will give a great deal of consideration to the deportment they will project when the television cameras are running. Perhaps that may be overcome in time, but I believe it will deteriorate into performances.
Then there is the other side of the coin. Our government and our parliament are something like our stomachs. Between elections they probably function best when you are least aware of their being there. Certainly between elections you do have to make some decisions that may not be popular. This applies to functions of government, of business, and even in one's own private affairs. One has to conduct himself in a way that it is not a continual case of doing everything he likes to do or everything that is popular.
Furthermore, I do not believe parliament functions best when there is a series of spectacular performances. Even this year there was a great deal of criticism of the budget simply because there was nothing spectacular in it. That in itself is not sufficient reason to criticize it.
If the government takes the position-and I do not say I do-that during the fiscal year 1963 the proposals it brought in did in fact set Canada on a new course, and that course was producing results, then there would be no need to have any spectacular changes.
I am waiting for the day when the impact of television performances begins to wane because I do not believe there is much relationship between your television image and your actual administrative ability. The one is not related to the other, although this matter of how you appear on television, and the number of times you appear on it, has a great deal to do with whether you get elected or not.
That is all I have to say so far as we are concerned. We are willing to support the setting up of a committee to give the matter some consideration, and perhaps even to go as far as having it on a trial basis, but I personally am also of the opinion that parliament is a little over-publicized even now.

Would you say that is why you are making your speech now?

Mr. Speaker, I am very delighted to see the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) back with us because he has been absent for some time. We know that reporting in the press gallery sometimes does not reflect too accurately what we consider is important in parliament. We also know some of the press gallery reporting coverage appears to encourage the antics of some members; but to be quite fair we can also agree that reporting by members of the press is effective in cutting down members who somewhat abuse their privileges in the house.
I do not know whether we could devise an equitable way in which the proceedings of the house could be televised. Many problems immediately arise, such as the time to be apportioned between the government and the various opposition groups; but in general I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Greenwood deserves to be entertained seriously.
We have also to remember that we are dealing with a controlled media where, at best, we have probably only two competing stations in any particular area. The danger of increasing the role of such a controlled media is somewhat frightening, taking into account the influences of advertisers and, if we are to believe the suggestions of some hon. members, the influence of politics and perhaps of future governments.

In raising this point I want to make it clear there is no other news media that is so closely regulated and controlled by so few. In my opinion the advantage which newspapers and periodicals hold over television lies in their ability to cover the news and the political scene in a way television never can, and we have to appreciate the fact that continually several points of view are being projected by these other media. This unique role that the periodicals and newspapers maintain, and which they have as an advantage over television and radio, has enabled them to maintain their competitive position in covering the news. Having raised this point, I should like to say that I strongly support the legislation now on the order paper to regelate advertising in foreign magazines. At the same time I wish to express my equally strong disappointment at the provision excluding Time and Reader's Digest. I urge the government to reconsider its decision and I hope it will delete the clause excluding these two publications before the legislation is proceeded with. I do not think any member of the house could seriously quarrel with the fact that these publications are engaged in a dumping procedure as far as Canada is concerned, and I do not think anyone would seriously suggest that they reflect a truly Canadian viewpoint. Finally, may I say that in my opinion this motion has a great deal of merit and should be referred to the appropriate committee for study. I should like again to commend the hon. member for introducing it.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this resolution may I say I am very much against it on two counts. First of all, I think that people generally have some misapprehension today as to the functions of parliament. I think it would be well to examine the British system because under that system there are no desks in the chamber. There are places to which you go but no desks are assigned, and they have made their House of Commons a chamber of debate.
There is a feeling across the country, which I think might grow if our proceedings were televised, that units; members are warming the green leather seats in the Ho se of Commons they are not performing their functions as members of parliament. I do not agree that this is the sole function of a member. Basically the function of parliament is to be a chamber for debating our principles, our policies and also legislation.


The functions of a member of parliament are many in number. One of his functions is to be present during debates when he finds it necessary, I suppose. We are all guilty of some parochialism in regard to the areas from which we come. Those from the prairies may not be too interested in some of the industries of other parts of the country, so they may be discharging other duties. They may be attending committees or in their offices. In fact, we may even be outside of Ottawa altogether. It seems to me that our function is not to present our personal opinions here and I do not know how we can express the opinions of our constituents, whether we represent 260,000 or 60,000, unless we keep in contact with them.
I believe that at one time the province of Saskatchewan broadcast the proceedings of its legislature over the radio, but I do not think it is done today. I understand it was not very satisfactory and if our proceedings were televised I do not believe it would be very satisfactory. I ask this question: What network would want to carry the proceedings of the House of Commons day after day and, if it did so, would it be very profitable to it? How many viewers would there be? There are many times when we are in committee of the whole or engaged in other debates when the people of Canada, I believe, would not want to view the proceedings.
Then there is the human nature aspect. There is talk about delays in parliament. I have only been here since 1958 but whether the Liberals, the New Democratic party or the Social Credit party are the main opposition, I do not think there is going to be much change in the proceedings of the House of Commons from year to year unless we get down to amending the rules that govern debate in parliament.
I think we are all guilty of one thing. When the Liberals sat over here and we were over there, the situation was reversed. I am certain that the splinter parties are no more holy or moral politically, and if one of them happened to form the government the situation would be no different. I am sure that many members agree we have to get down to amending the rules of the House of Commons. If the rules were amended there might then be something to view, but there is no question that at the present time there are serious procedural delays. Sometimes these delays are misunderstood. I think it would be a sad and sorry day for democracy if the people of Canada, unless they had had the opportunity to become familiar with the situation through election to parliament, could walk into a room and view a debate on television, and be expected from viewing it to understand what parliament is about.

I repeat that parliament is a place where we debate principles and policies. If we had a camera here today it would not matter which side of the house was shown, although one corner may be a little better populated this afternoon than the others. However, I do not think that group can make any particular claim, because as far as absenteeism is concerned for the purpose of being in one's office or performing other duties I think the record of one party is just about the same as that of any other party.

I do not believe one should go into anything personal in a debate and I am not going to do so. Seriously, as far as I am concerned I cannot believe that the people of Canada want to view exactly what is on that side of the house at the present time, empty seats, and what is on this side, also some empty seats. They probably would not appreciate that, after all, we are merely debating a private member's notice of motion. For example, when I was absent from the House of Commons-
May I ask the hon. member a question? Does he not realize that if we had television of these proceedings the spotlight would be on him at this moment and not upon the empty seats around him?

That might be the greatest mistake television ever made, Mr. Speaker. This is what I am afraid of. These prima donnas to my left would always be talking because they would want to have their "physogs" before the camera to show what hardworking members of parliament they are and what great reformers they have been since the time of confederation.
I just want to complete one point before the question is put. The proceedings of the house have to be thoroughly understood and I think they can only be understood if one spends some time in the House of Commons or in the press gallery or in the public galleries. Things are misunderstood. For example, a week ago the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) brought in a private bill which 20220-133

Many people I talked to really believed there was a bill before the House of Commons to abolish the Senate, which might be passed. Very few people appreciated that there is only one hour each day for private bills. They thought it was government bill or a bill that would really be debated for weeks with the result that the Senate would either be abolished or not abolished.
I think there would be greater misunderstanding if people just viewed certain proceedings of the House of Commons because they would get the wrong idea. That is my feeling about the matter and it is supported by the experience in Saskatchewan where the C.C.F. government of that day instituted broadcasting of the proceedings of the legislature by radio. They gave it up because they found it was not very satisfactory. After the novelty wore off people were not too interested. I suppose that televising the proceedings might possibly clear up some misunderstandings. However, last week the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) made a speech in Lethbridge. He said there had been some delay in the proceedings of the house, with the result that the government had not been able to proceed with its farm legislation, which was on the order paper, and get it passed. I have looked at the order paper and I cannot find any farm legislation. I suppose what he was doing was more or less bluffing about the proceedings on the basis of the debate on the supplementary estimates. I do not believe the putting of the proceedings of this House of Commons on television is going to clear up that misunderstanding. In fact, I would say it would only add to the confusion.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

No, I should like to finish what I have to say. You have had time to make your speech, so I would like to complete my remarks. If the house would like to adopt this motion, 1 should like to see it given an opportunity to go on record in that regard.
Basically, I believe the adoption of this scheme would only add to the confusion. Surely, there is enough confusion now. This is illustrated by the things we read in newspapers about what really goes on in parliament. There is no doubt about it, so far as a member of the house is concerned and the members of the various political parties, the political image is still important. As hon. members know, there was a book written about one prime minister, and I would invite hon. members to read about the myth built up about the late President Kennedy. It is rather interesting to read the history of that

Royal Assent
situation. I suppose the book was withheld from publication because of the tragedy that took place last year. There is no doubt about it, a myth was built up. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that television would help in creating a false image of parliament in the minds of the Canadian people. So far as I am concerned, I oppose this motion on that basis and I oppose any legislation arising out of it.

I recall that when the debate proceeded before, certain adjectives were used about the budget. I think it was described as a "stand pat" budget, a "do nothing" budget, and I propose to add a few phrases of description of my own. The budget seems to me to be a budget of creeping complacency; it is conservative to the core. I use that word not in the political sense but in the proper meaning of the word conservative. I see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) blanch as I use these words.

speechtext:
"Squirm" is the word that my colleague suggests. At any rate, it is appropriate to the occasion. This budget is a declaration of neutrality in the war against poverty. It accepts the sterile orthodoxies of the 1930's. It fails altogether to employ the fiscal remedies available to deal with the present day problems-problems of growth and of unemployment. At a time when we urgently need federal leadership we get this uninspiring, negative and deadening budget. At a time when we need to move firmly forward, we are invited to stand still. Those are a few of the adjectives that I think can properly be added to describe this budget.
One could almost hear the sigh of relief with which the government accepted as an excuse for inaction the stimulus to the economy of the purely fortuitous sales of wheat to countries behind the iron curtain. It is our belief that the budget could be, and should be, an important instrument to be used aggressively to promote expansion, to cure unemployment and to remove unnecessary poverty. It is our conviction that it will be found impossible to change over the Canadian economy to rapid and steady growth and full employment without taking vigorous measures to induce greater equality of opportunity and standards of living for Canadians. To put it in other words, if we moved vigorously to meet the most urgent unfilled needs of fellow Canadians, we would at the same time be giving an impetus to our whole

economy. The pursuit of social justice will lead to economic progress. There may be some who question whether or not we have in Canada serious destitution, poverty or deprivation. In our affluent North American society much poverty is hidden. There can, however, be no doubt that it is real.
A well known Swedish economist, Mr. Gunnar Myrdal, in his recent book "Challenge to Affluence" has outlined the situation in the United States. He documented the continuing pockets of poverty in that most prosperous and affluent society. He points out that the bureau of census, several of the departments in Washington and of the state administrations, university institutions and other research outfits have in recent years done a commendable job of laying bare the facts of American poverty and of the causal relations behind this poverty. I commend to hon. members opposite the most fascinating statistical review I have ever read-perhaps the only fascinating statistical review I have ever read-called "Rich Man, Poor Man" by Herman P. Miller, special assistant to the United States bureau of statistics. I would suggest to some aspiring Canadian statistician that he should write such a book and do the same thing for Canada as Mr. Miller did for the United States. We do not appear to have up to date information available in Canada, although some significant facts can be obtained from income tax statistics. Some of these were presented to the house in this debate by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow); others, to which I will refer later, are to be found in a report of the research projects section of the dominion bureau of statistics for the year 1957.
It is highly probable that the conclusions arrived at by Professor Myrdal and Mr. Miller about the United States are roughly comparable to the conditions which exist in Canada. Professor Myrdal based his conclusions on a condensation of various studies derived from "Poverty and deprivation in the United States", published by the conference on economic progress. He defined "poverty" for multiple-persons families as having to live on a family income of under $4,000 a year; and for unattached individuals, under $2,000 a year. On this definition 38 million Americans-or more than one fifth of the nation-were poor in 1960. Similar figures in Canada would mean that between three million and four million Canadians fall below the poverty line. In the United States another 39 million were below what Professor Myrdal calls the "deprivation line", that is to say had incomes, for families, between $4,000 and $6,000, and for individuals between $2,000 20220-133J
The Budget-Mr. Brewin and $3,000. He uses another term, "destitution"; that is to say, the situation of people with less than half of the income representing the poverty line. This destitution was the destiny of more than 12J million Americans, or nearly 7 per cent of the population of the United States.
A similar figure for Canada would be over 1J million. The groups which in the United States of America are afflicted by poverty are the minorities, such as the non-whites, small farmers and farm workers, the people from 65 years of age upward, the less well educated and the unemployed, and 40 per cent of the families whose heads were unemployed were living in poverty. Poverty hits the family whose head is a female, the family which has lost a husband and father, or never had one. Long term unemployment is creating a class of unemployables. Even the figures of unemployment do not present a full picture, as many are under-employed, that is employed part-time, and many who could, in a full employment economy, be employed do not enter the labour market.
I have no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian poverty can be found in similar groups. I am particularly concerned about destitution among older people. The survey conducted by the research projects section of the dominion bureau of statistics which I have already referred to indicates that approximately one quarter of the heads of families and unattached individuals over 65 throughout Canada, other than farmers, had cash incomes of less than $1,000 a year in 1957 and that this figure reached in the prairie provinces nearly one half of the families and individuals.
I do not have available the figures to fit into Professor Myrdal's analysis of destitution, but it is clear that destitution is the common fate of most Canadians over 65. Indeed, the average income of families-this is of whole families-with heads aged 65 or over was $2,535 for Canada, and as low as $1,830 for the prairie provinces.
It may be asked; What can the budget do about this? The first thing to be recognized is that redistributional reform is necessary from the point of view of social justice. Redistributional reform involves a reduction in the tax burden on persons in the lower income brackets, as well as the imposition of the capital gains tax as suggested by my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron).
I know, Mr. Speaker, that there is a royal commission on taxation which has not yet reported, but I venture to say that no royal commission on taxation is needed to demonstrate the injustice of maintaining income tax on persons with an income which is in

The Budget-Mr. Brewin fact so low as to put them below a reasonable definition of poverty. In 1961, the last year for which figures are available to me, there were 2,495,168 taxpayers with incomes of less than $4,000, who paid a total tax of $387.4 million. To remove the tax burden from the backs of those already suffering from poverty in an affluent society would be an act of social justice which it would be well within the capacity of the government to undertake immediately. But the argument for such a reduction in taxation at the lower levels is not merely to benefit the poor. This tax reduction would be equally as important as a basis for the achievement of expansion of the economy. It would be of general economic interest and not only benefit the poor themselves. Unemployment and the lower productivity of the lower income brackets is one of our major unutilized and under-utilized resources.
Is it not possible, Mr. Speaker, for us to have the good sense to see that a real effort to relieve those in need is, according to the best economic advice we can get, also part of economic wisdom? In the United States of America the government has accepted the notion of an unremitting war on poverty. Our government should at least be as equally committed to such a war. It could perhaps take a look at the American example of tax cutting. A substantial tax cut suggested by the President of the United States was accepted by congress as a necessary means of stimulating a relatively stagnant economy. A proportionate tax cut in Canada would amount to roughly $500 million. Our economy has at least been equally as stagnant as the United States economy. Why has the government rejected a similar stimulus to the Canadian economy? The tax cut approved by congress in the United States was, in accordance with the American pattern, not applied at the lower levels only. It is my contention that if a tax cut of half a billion dollars were applied by the Canadian government and applied at the lower levels of income, the increased demand would give a tremendous and urgently needed stimulus to the Canadian economy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are two other matters I would like to mention. I was very greatly disappointed at the announcement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on Friday that the federal government was not going to increase its contribution to hospital construction. I found one of the reasons he gave particularly disturbing. He said that one or more provinces had objected. If, Mr. Speaker, there is a grave crisis affecting the lives and health of a very large section of Canada-there is no doubt that there is and
CMr. Brewin.]

I could spend much time documenting the case-is the veto of some province or provinces to prevent federal action? The Prime Minister, in my judgment, has shown weakness in sheltering behind the objection of one or two provinces.
The statement that hospitals are a provincial responsibility is indeed true; but the existence of the present federal hospital grants is a recognition that a federal contribution is in order. If it is to be made at all, why should it not be increased to keep up with increasing costs and to aid in relieving a very real and grave crisis? Because the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) and myself have been consistently pressing for federal relief in this field, an impression has developed that this is a local Toronto matter. It is nothing of the sort. It is a matter seriously affecting every urban and metropolitan centre.
We are glad to hear in this house about the special needs of other areas-Quebec, the maritimes, the prairies, the Yukon, and so on. I hope the government does not think that it should ignore the needs and requests of major metropolitan areas, which in numbers alone exceed most of the provinces. It will be making a great mistake if it does.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is one more subject I should like to mention if I have time. I should like to say a few words about another notable document which was brought before the house since the budget was introduced, and I refer to the white paper on defence. It is very obviously related to the budget as it contemplates continuing defence expenditures of more than $1.5 billion a year. Obviously I have not time to discuss the white paper in detail. It has received a very good press, and the impression has been created, not I must say from any careful reading of the white paper itself, that the machinery of integration which it proposes and which has been highlighted represents a substantial saving, and that the proposals of the white paper taken together would, if carried into effect, bring about a substantial lightening of the burden of defence expenditure. Nothing could be further from the truth. Indeed, the gains on the swings are more than made up on the roundabouts. At page 24 of the white paper-I will not have time to read it

are serious proposals for additional major expenditures.
The fact is that the white paper is a very serious disappointment. It puts some new and welcome emphasis on Canada's peace keeping role and the mobile forces required to fulfil it. It talks of the obsolescence of strategic concepts and then provides for Canada to continue its part in the obsolete

and indeed dangerous concept of tactical nuclear weapons to be used in response to any aggression in Europe. The search for the new and more realistic and effective role that the Prime Minister in his famous Scarborough speech of January 1963, saw as the result of promise of re-examination, turns out to be a mirage. The truth is that the white paper tries to do the impossible. It clings to the old love and seeks to embrace the new at the same time. It cannot do both. It cannot sustain an effective mobile intervention role in NATO and for the United Nations, and at the same time maintain our share of the forward forces by supplying a brigade group and air force squadrons for the front line in Europe.
The white paper falls between two stools. The bold, new look that was promised has been compromised by the conservatism which has prevented a break with the past. The real dilemma has not been solved. We are going to proceed with the continuing futility of doing a little of everything that is involved. The white paper poses the question of whether our role should be a nuclear or a non-nuclear one, and then evades it.
The white paper talks of flexibility. I hope this means that the minister and his advisers will move forward from the very small advance they have made, as represented in the white paper. I can assure the Minister of Finance, if he needs assurance, that until they do, until they move forward from trying to do a little bit of everything, as the white paper suggests, his problems of rising defence expenditures will grow, and not diminish, as the years go by.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words in this debate and perhaps, like the hon. member who preceded me, I too may stray a little from the subject of the budget.
At the outset may I say I was pleased with the reference made by the Minister of Finance to the extension of family allowances to the 16 and 17 year old students still in school. I was also encouraged by his reference to a student loan plan because this represents a great improvement. I do not think I would go far as to say it is an unprecedented step, but certainly it shows a welcome attention being paid by the federal government to the problems of the youth of the country.
Certainly in the whole field of social security this government is to be congratulated for at least showing its willingness to bring in some new legislation. Indeed, the Canada pension plan represents the first new, major piece of social security legislation in all too long a period. Because of this I am hopeful that the present administration will
The Budget-Mr. Cashin come to grips with all, or most, of the present inequities that exist at the present time within the framework of our social security laws.
Our social security laws were bred in the desperate thirties. Since then we have increased them and one might even say, begrudgingly at times extended them. Unfortunately, however, there has evolved a non-planned, often unrelated patchwork system. The time has come for all of us, at this level of government and at other levels of government, to ascertain just what we are doing in this field because, as was pointed out in the debate earlier this afternoon, for all of our brave talk and for all of our eloquent speeches there is still a great deal to be accomplished. Relatively, I say relatively, Mr. Speaker, do we know how much better off are those in the lower income group today than they were 30 years ago.
I am alarmed, Mr. Speaker, because there are many Canadians who, consciously or subconsciously, feel that we have done enough in this field of social security. They feel this, I am convinced, without ever having studied the inequities that exist within the framework of our present approach.
