speechtext:
No party is without blame in this field-none of us.
We have just increased the old age pension and I submit that the figure of $75 per month is at best only supplementary to the income of our retired citizens, and because of that we are attempting to introduce the Canada pension plan. However, the pension is a considerable amount compared to the miserly allowances paid to the widows in our country. I suggest that we examine what the ten provinces of Canada are paying to widows. They are and form a whole class of people who have to apply for this allowance, but there is not one province that proportionately comes close in equalling the allowance to widows to that given to old age pensioners.
I would suggest that at the forthcoming conference of welfare ministers, in the spirit of co-operative federalism, all levels of government try to determine what we can accomplish as a nation, not just as ten provinces, to remove the awful inequities that exist in our haphazard approach to social security.
One great obstacle to a fundamental understanding of social security must be removed. Social security is not taking from the rich and giving to the poor; it is not a form of charity. It is, more often than not, a transfer of income from individual to individual within the same group. For example, the worker with no children helps to pay for the

The Budget-Mr. Cashin worker in the same group who has eight or nine children, and the worker who is healthy helps to pay for the benefits that the sick receive.
We must recognize that in our advanced technological society there are many things which we consume collectively, and which we can only consume if we consume them collectively. It is folly to suggest that we live in an era of private consumption and private earning, or that we should return to such an age. To do this, or to say this, is to ignore the scientific revolution that has come about in the last several decades. It is amazing that with each suggestion of a further improvement in our social security laws the same old arguments are raised against them. There is probably not one reasonable person in Canada who would suggest that we remove the social security legislation now on the statute books, but when additional legislation is advocated, and quite often the additional legislation represents only a compromise, the laissez-faire arguments that were applicable to the 19th century situation are applied to the 20th century situation. This shows a desire on the part of some to protect a narrow, vested interested. It also shows a failure to recognize the great changes wrought in the last several decades.
You may recall, Mr. Speaker, that the Canada pension plan was opposed last year. I have very good reason to question not only the motives but many of the arguments advanced against it. But if we think the opposition to the Canada pension plan is anything, what is going to happen when the government eventually gets around to giving us that much needed piece of legislation, a comprehensive medical program? The government will then find itself in a tough position, with one group saying it does not go far enough, and another group not knowing what to say but nevertheless criticizing us, while at the same time we have 19 million Canadians not greatly interested in those viewpoints because all they want is to see such a plan in operation. Yet we, who sometimes seem to think the whole world is watching us from the gallery, interested in every word we say, will probably delay the implementation of such a program for several years.
I have referred to the 19th century attitude that resurrects itself whenever we talk about social security. I expect it is a distorted notion of freedom. We in the 1960's can be truly more free than man ever dreamed of 100, or even 30 years ago. Because of our scientific advancements and our great breakthroughs in medicine, we now have in the sum total of human knowledge the ways and means to live better, to live longer, and to

live in better health. But to apply 19th century thinking to this type of society means that all free men will not be free to enjoy the benefits of mankind's achievements. Many of these achievements, Mr. Speaker, can only be available to you and to me if they are available to all men.
Let us understand the meaning of social security and the function of social security in the 1960's. It is not to be confused with creeping socialism, and we must not allow ourselves to be retarded in our progress because of a misunderstanding of what social security laws are all about. It is not to be confused with the government's control of the economy through control of the means of production, though it does represent certain government intervention in the economy, but since the days of Keynes this has become fashionable, if not always understood. It follows that the state is merely an instrument or agency through which these things can be accomplished. Theoretically, at least, the state is not the only available agency, but practically I suggest it is.
I have already made reference to the inequities in our present social security system, and have given as a specific example the widows' allowances. There are a great many others. If we are to talk about social security we must talk in terms of defining our philosophy of social security, and if we look at it in the light of the functions of society I think we will remove the argument that this is a continuing handout program. This concept of a handout program has arisen because successive governments have not had the courage to understand it themselves, and in that sense the politicians of the past 30 years are somewhat to blame.
With regard to social security I am interested, of course, in seeing that we have national standards, and this presumes a strong central government. I believe we can only have equalization of opportunity for all Canadians if in fact we have a strong federal system. While I am on the subject I may say I realize that in the province of Quebec our brother Canadians of the French tongue are concerned at the present moment about equalization of opportunity. It seems to me that all Canadians are in sympathy with their aspirations and are sincerely interested. But, Mr. Speaker, some views-I hope they represent nothing like a majority-held by responsible men in the province of Quebec would suggest that we have a dilemma to be resolved because these people feel that the only way the province of Quebec can fulfil its aspirations is through a weakening of the fiscal authority of the federal government. On the other side of the coin there are areas, not as well to do at all as the province of Quebec, that are

quite convinced that the only way we can achieve equalization of opportunity is through a strong federal system.
For a moment I should like to present a hypothetical situation of a Canada exactly the same as it is today except in one respect, that one respect being that all of the 10 provinces have the same mother tongue. What would the differences be between that Canada and the real Canada? The Atlantic provinces situated as they are on the extremity of Canada would be in the same economic position as they are today. That being the case, the federal government and the well to do areas of Canada would have the challenge to help create an atmosphere in which the Atlantic provinces could develop. The same quid pro quo would exist between the extremities and the centre of this country as now exists. In the centre the great industries, being protected, would find outlets for their industries in the extremities.
We might ask ourselves what the position of the province of Quebec would be in this hypothetical Canada where we were all of one language. Would the education system be the same? If not, what effect would that have? In this example, of course the means of production, industry and commerce in that hypothetical Quebec would be owned by people of the same mother tongue and the same culture as the working people. We might ask ourselves whether in that imaginary Canada I have conceived Quebec would still be second only to the Atlantic provinces in unemployment.
I have used this example, perhaps a very crude one, to come to the point about which I am wondering. Who are the people who can say best at this time what is the answer to the dilemma I posed a few minutes ago with regard to those who see the federal system a little differently than I do? I might suggest with a great deal of support, I am sure, that perhaps if the federal government had even stronger powers than those that some would now take away, what is now happening in the province of Quebec would have happened 40 years ago or perhaps would not have happened at all, because of the existence of a truly strong federal government.
I have been talking about the federal government theme, and I do so because if we are to have national standards and a sound approach to social security I believe we must have a strong federal government. But I am concerned that when we talk about national unity and the powers of the federal government we may find ourselves in 15 or 20 years, having spent a great deal of time talking about these matters, actually confronted more forcibly than we are now with
The Budget-Mr. Cashin what may be the real underlying problem, the United States of America, and whether or not we will remain economically and politically independent of that country to the south. If the Atlantic provinces or any one of the areas on the extremities need a strong central government to help to bring about equalization of opportunities, I suggest the argument is just as strong that so do the 10 provinces of Canada under that government unless, of course, we are to accept what some suggest is the real question, that economically and politically we might be better off if we did not exist in this form at all.
So far as higher standards of social security are concerned I have noted, as some other hon. members may also have noted, a book by Michael Harrington, "The Other America" in which he suggests that in the United States of America there are 40 million to 50 million Americans living at a bare subsistence level. If we compare Canada with the United States we find that our standard of living is 25 per cent to 30 per cent behind that country. If in the United States they have 40 million to 50 million Americans living at a subsistence level, I think it would be reasonable to assume that the comparable figure is higher in Canada although, as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) pointed out in his remarks, the proper kind of study of this problem that we would like to have has not been made in our country.
In the United States recently there has been much discussion about the war on poverty. Senator Fulbright, who is one of the more enlightened of contemporary American political figures, said recently in a speech at the University of North Carolina that the war on poverty is only beginning. In fact he criticized his countrymen in a sense for their preoccupation with the cold war, induced by an hysteria that has lingered as a hangover from the McCarthy era. He suggested that more attention needs to be paid to the problems of social security.
Perhaps the analogy has some value in regard to what I was talking about a moment ago. While we may be pursuing a very vital and necessary course in indulging in introspection about our national identity and culture, it may be that this is being done at the expense of our resources and creativeness just as in the United States the cold war, as Senator Fulbright has suggested, has affected that country.
In talking about equalization of opportunity, and social security would be a part of that grandiose phrase, the traditional outlook has been, of course, that, rural areas are continually attempting to bring themselves up to urban standards. But I am quite convinced, as I feel most of us are, that perhaps some of

The Budget-Mr. honey the greatest human misery that exists in this country exists within the very heartland of our cities. The problems of urban growth and urban renewal are just as important because poverty is just as harsh and in some cases perhaps harsher in our cities than in rural areas.
The problem of urban renewal is one that again necessitates, I suggest, national policies and national standards. Many hon. members on both sides of the house have enumerated programs which would have national implications to raise our economic standards, and standards of living. As has been mentioned earlier in the debate, the government has made a start on some of these things. It has made a start unprecedented for Canada in bringing forth legislation relative to planning, and the creation of the Department of Industry is something that represents a significant step forward. I hope that an enlightened federal approach to the problem of urban renewal will be another that will be forthcoming.
This afternoon we listened to a speech by the distinguished member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart). It is obvious that the way the name of that constituency is bandied about by some of the less informed members of the house, they do not know how to pronounce it correctly as we do. We know that this afternoon this very distinguished member enumerated some of the programs and policies which this government has started, and some of the things which they have not yet started but which we hope they will start. These programs will affect the equalization of opportunities for those of us from the Atlantic provinces.
Now, I have talked about social security and about a strong federal government with national standing. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that having been here for some time, perhaps not as long as most hon. members in this house, I have come to the conclusion that the greatest challenge that faces Canada today is not biculturalism. The greatest challenge that faces us is the eradication of poverty and the equalization of opportunity for all Canadians in all provinces. We should make sure that Canada and Canadians keep abreast of changing conditions in our increasingly scientific and technological world. We will find then that biculturalism and bilingualism will become only part of this greater problem.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In participating in this budget debate, I wish to say at the outset that it is my intention to confine my remarks to matters of immediate concern within the riding of Bruce. In dealing with these matters, I shall address my remarks to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets). While
my remarks, in essence, might appear to the minister to be criticism, I would remind him that as the elected representative of the riding of Bruce I speak for and on behalf of the constituents of that riding and the matters of concern that affect the people of the riding, and the welfare of the people.
One matter of immediate concern which I would present to the minister for reconsideration is the dredging of the harbour at Kincardine. I refer now to a letter written to the minister on October 16, 1963, in which I ask, with reference to a dredging program, "when will a dredging program be undertaken to improve the harbour facilities at Kincardine." I quote from the minister's reply of October 23, 1963:
It is considered that existing depths in the harbour are adequate for the normal traffic. Therefore, it is not planned to undertake any dredging program at this place.
I draw attention, Mr. Speaker, to the words "are adequate for the normal traffic". I have here a letter from fishermen operating out of the harbour at Kincardine, dated March 3, 1964. I quote:
We the undersigned fishermen, holding valid commercial fishing licences out of the harbour situated at Kincardine, Ontario and district, respectfully petition to have the harbour at Kincardine dredged.
We believe that it should be deepened to a depth navigable by fishing craft, and also yachts and smaller craft which are very numerous during the summer season. At the present time the harbour is not navigable by any craft with a draft greater than four feet. We respectfully submit that it should be deepened to a depth not less than nine or ten feet.
The present condition of this harbour, prevents it being used by any craft caught on the lake by a storm, the majority of fishing craft in this area have a draft of seven feet.
This letter is signed by D. A. MacLeod; Charles L. Pilon; Roy F. Jackson; William R. Jackson and F. B. Rayner. These men are all licensed commercial fishermen operating out of the harbour at Kincardine.
The immediate need for dredging is caused by the current low water level of the great lakes. The drop is now close to three feet. In addition, there is the natural silting from the Penetangore river which flows into the harbour basin. The town of Kincardine is very much aware of the resultant silting action and has endeavoured to convince the Department of Public Works of the benefits of a control dam. These efforts were unsuccessful, and I should like to quote from a reply the town received from the Department of Public Works. It is addressed to Mr. C. Roy Whiting, chairman, town planning board, corporation of the town of Kincardine. I quote from the text:
Of the three purposes or benefits mentioned in your letter that would result from the construc-
[Mr. Cashin.j

tion of the dam, only the prevention of the harbour silting up would be of interest to this department. In this regard, our annual cost to maintain the harbour for its present use amounts to less than $3,000. Furthermore, the percentage of this average cost, due to settlement of river materials as distinct from materials entering from the lake, are not known. Also the ability of the proposed dam to retain the river silt would depend largely on the design and can only be determined by a detailed study to establish the amount of silt being carried down and the amount that would still pass through the dam during periods of heavy flow.
Although the capital cost of the dam, including expropriation, etc., and its operating costs, have not been calculated, it would appear that any savings, if any, in our maintenance dredging as a result of the dam would be extremely small and, therefore, any participation in this project by this department could not be justified.
Mr. Speaker, this reply sets out in detail the small annual cost of the maintenance of the harbour which is essential to the fishing craft, a shelter during storms, a tourist attraction, and the mainstay in the economy of a resort town. I have here a resolution passed by the Kincardine town council, indicating they are aware of the existing situation. This resolution is dated March 10, 1964, and reads as follows:
That the council request the clerk to write a letter to the Department of Public Works requesting that the Kincardine harbour be dredged and some form of renovating program be carried out in 1964.
This resolution is signed by R. Lauten-slager, clerk-treasurer. The Kincardine harbour is a natural stopover for yachtsmen, since it is approximately halfway between Sarnia and Tobermory. The business community has worked hard for many years to attract this trade and it is of the utmost importance that harbour facilities be available. I should like to put on the record two letters from businessmen who service pleasure craft with fuel and supplies. This letter is dated March 10 and is addressed to the Minister of Public Works. I quote:
May we take the liberty to petition you and your department to give serious consideration of dredging the harbour at Kincardine this spring?
I have gasoline pumps at the government dock and last year we had between 450 and 500 yachts; most of these yachts were from the U.S.A. and they leave large sums of American currency each year in Canada. Mr. Cottrill, who is my competitor, also had a number of yachts at his marina.
As you likely know, we are situated just about half-way between Sarnia and Tobermory. This makes a nice run from Sarnia to Kincardine in a day and then from Kincardine to Tobermory the next day. For the last number of years the boating has been on the increase and it will continue to do so, however, we must help the cause along by giving the boating people good harbours. I understand that the states are fixing their harbours so as to keep the boaters on the American side of the great lakes.
Goderich has a good harbour, but it is a commercial port and some of the boaters do not like the noise, etc.
The Budget-Mr. Loney
From a safety point of view there is a stretch of about 60 to 70 miles between Goderich and Port Elgin where, if a sudden storm came up, there would be no haven for a boat to seek shelter except Kincardine, and with the shallow water at Kincardine it would be difficult for a fair sized boat to get into our harbour. Some of the fishermen tell me that they will have trouble getting their fishing tugs into Kincardine this year.
Therefore, sir, we here in Kincardine would appreciate very much if you would consider our request and have the harbour dredged to a depth of about 10 to 12 feet and have the pilings around the harbour checked.
Yours sincerely, Clarence H. Walpole.
I wish, now, to quote a second letter which is also addressed to the Minister of Public Works. This letter is dated March 14, 1964. It says:
We are writing in support of a plea that some dredging be done at our harbour in Kincardine, Ontario.
We realize that our harbour is used for small pleasure craft and that we have upwards of 600 yachts each summer. These yachts are over 90 per cent from the American side and constitute a large part of our tourist trade. The tourist trade has always been one of our main industries and we are naturally interested in seeing that we have proper facilities to look after it. Unless we have 10 to 12 feet of water in our harbour there are many yachts and fishing tugs which will have difficulty. Many yachts are sailing craft and these, by their type of construction, draw considerable water, even small ones. We should also like to point out that as a harbour for storm shelter we do not have enough water to admit fair sized craft.
We do hope you will give consideration to dredging at this time.
Sincerely yours,
James C. D. Cottrill.
The low water level is of serious consequence to the lakeshore tourist areas of western Ontario. Recently, the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) and the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Noble) brought this to the attention of the house. I have here a picture published in the Wiarton Echo on March 26 showing a dock at Wiarton which is completely above the waterline. There is a late model car parked on the dry ground beside the dock. As further evidence of the seriousness of the low water situation I have the April 8 issue of the Port Elgin Times. On the front page is a picture of the dock at Port Elgin. Underneath, it says:
The receding waters of the great lakes and especially the Georgian bay and lake Huron area are causing considerable concern among the lake-shore communities. The lowest ever, might mean fewer yachts stay-over in Port Elgin this year. This photo, taken from the lakeshore road area towards the small craft catwalk and the Bluewater tearoom, shows how far down the water has gone this past year.
From the same issue of the Port Elgin Times I should like to quote the caption
2116	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Loney beneath another photograph of government property at Port Elgin. The picture shows a breakwa'll which is high and dry above the waterline. There is no water in sight at all. The caption reads:
The south breakwall Is presently high and dry at the local beach as the water level dropped another two feet this year.
This is further evidence of the seriousness of the situation. Also from Port Elgin comes a picture beneath which appears the following caption:
Here are three craft attempting to turn around to come back into the local harbor. The boats were out some distance past the breakwalls, but low water levels allowed spectators to walk out right up to the stuck craft most of them making their way along the stoney bar shown above.
This is further indication of the gravity of the situation in the lakeshore area. I have another picture showing the Southampton harbour with an article stating the intention of the local residents. This is from the Southampton Beacon.
The Georgian Bay development association has begun a serious survey of the water levels of the Georgian bay and lake Huron.
Because of the serious eifects of the present record low levels of these waters, commercial trade is suffering in several ports and hundreds of cottagers as well as commercial enterprises are finding their docks even higher out of water.
Numerous examples of this devastating effect can be noted at establishments along the shore lines and to stay in business this year thousands of dollars will have to be spent by the owners.
Neville Keefe, general manager of the association, told this paper that the association's first move would be general discussion with government officials and other agencies as to the causes of the recession of the waters, and a survey of the effects of this on the economy of the areas affected.
The low water level presented problems last year as well. I refer now to the launching ramp at the government dock at Dyer's Bay. Last year the local residents found it necessary to extend at their own expense-I repeat: at their own expense-the small craft landing ramp leading to the receding waterline. I was informed by the secretary of the Dyer's Bay resort association that the extension they built last year is now six feet from the waterline. I intend to speak on this matter on another occasion. The problems resulting from the current low water level are evident at all government docks on the shoreline of Bruce. Immediate attention should be given to the harbour facilities at Port Elgin and Southampton.
It was with dismay that we learned in Bruce of the decision of the present administration to cancel the proposed dredging project at the Sauble river. This program involved some $60,000 and was absolutely 

necessary to the maintenance of the tourist industry in this resort area.
To return to the situation at Kincardine harbour, I would ask the minister to give serious consideration to the numerous requests for a dredging program. In addition, the department should investigate the damage being done to pleasure craft by the pilings which are now above the waterline. We would also ask the minister to consider the petitions of the community for the construction of a small craft launching ramp. The minister stated in his reply of November 19, 1963 that he would have engineers examine a site if there were reasons to warrant an expenditure, and I now present for his consideration petitions of the chamber of commerce of Kincardine. These petitions are addressed to myself, and the first is dated March 28, 1964.
The Kincardine and district chamber of commerce urgently request that you plead with your government on our behalf, for the erection of a boat ramp in the vicinity of the harbour.
Your government wishes us to improve our tourist facilities in order to encourage more tourist dollars spent in Canada. We feel sure they will want to do their part to carry out this important program.
As lake Huron is the only geographical asset we have, it behooves us to make the most of it.
If we are assured work will be started on the ramp in the immediate future, we can advertise it to our prospective summer visitors.
May we have a definite answer immediately,
Very truly yours,
Mrs. J. Henderson Secretary-treasurer.
The second petition is dated April 2, 1964 and reads as follows:
I'm writing on behalf of the chamber of commerce with regard to the Department of Public Works building a boat launching ramp in Kincardine.
Situated as we are on lake Huron it is unthinkable that we should go through another summer without proper launching facilities. We have done a road check and we find that every fifth car has a boat and trailer. This check was done for us by our chief of police last July. Those who operate tourist accommodation tell me that there are many requests for a boat launching ramp. We in Kincardine are going all-out this summer to promote our tourist industry. This is more important to the life of our town because of the loss of two important industries. There are also many more boats in Kincardine and surrounding area than there has ever been.
To date we have been able to get a suitable site on the north side of the north pier, directly in front of the house occupied by Gordon Lafrance. There is much more ground work to be done in this regard. However, for now I think those of us from the chamber and the town council who have viewed the site agree that this is the most logical place. Also we have enlisted the help necessary to get the roadway built. This will be done by the town council. The chamber, although lacking in funds will do everything possible with regard to smooth operation of the ramp and with the normal upkeep of the site once it has been built.

Mr. Scroggie, the district engineer, from London had his Mr. George Metrink call on us and we have obtained some valuable information from him. They have been most co-operative and we appreciate the efforts they have made thus far.
That is signed "Jim Cottrill" on behalf of the tourist committee. Mr. Speaker, in concluding my remarks I ask the minister to reconsider his reply of October 23, 1963 with regard to a dredging program at the Kincardine harbour. I reiterate that reply:
It is considered that existing depths in the harbour are adequate for the normal traffic. Therefore it is not planned to undertake a dredging program at this place.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of those concerned, I ask that we be given the opportunity to substantiate our requests.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my remarks, allow me to congratulate the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay) on his recent appointment as Minister of Citizenship and Immigration for Canada. I will not wait any longer to wish him a fruitful career within the federal cabinet and in the administration of his department in particular.
The beautiful riding of Matapedia-Matane runs along the eastern side of the riding of Rimouski which I have the honour and the privilege to represent in the House of Commons of Canada.
If Rimouski is represented in the house by a member of the opposition, it has the enviable privilege of seeing two of its distinguished sons in the federal cabinet.
That is why, at this time, I must offer my thanks to the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson) for the great honour done to so many families connected with the hon. members for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Lamontagne) and for Matapedia-Matane.
In fact, the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean comes from Mont Joli, Rimouski county, and he too was appointed recently Secretary of State for Canada. As far as the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is concerned, he comes from Luceville, near the town of Rimouski.
The two cabinet ministers, who come from the Rimouski county, maintain probably a particular affection for the region of their respective origin. To every valiant heart, the nativeland is always dear, is it not?
With regard to the riding of Rimouski, it would be most ungrateful on my part to rise here and charge the federal government with discriminating against Rimouski voters and its representative. Facts are facts, and a careful study of the measures passed by Ottawa in favour of the riding of Rimouski bear witness to the solicitude of the federal 20220-1344
The Budget-Mr. Ouellet government in providing Rimouski with its full share of subsidies, grants, etc. Public works, harbour installations, subsidies to the ferry Pere Nouvel in service between Rimouski and the north shore, are amongst the main contributions of the federal government to my riding. Such a kind of cooperation is to the credit of the government. Speaking of co-operation, I would like to thank the hon. member for Saguenay (Mr. Blouin) for helping as concerns the proposals made with a view to solving the problem of the ferry between Rimouski and Baie Comeau.
I believe repairs and wharf installations at Pointe au Pere and Trois Pistoles will again be subsidized this year by the federal government. When the facilities become available the ferry Le Razade, which operates between Trois Pistoles and Les Escoumins, will give the required service which is necessary for the development of our region. Incidentally, when will a deep water wharf be built in Trois Pistoles? The existing wharf is situated on a ridge and requires the dredging operations which are bothersome for all parties concerned. It is said that a deep water wharf could be built at little expense about two miles east of the existing structure.
Trois Pistoles is a growing maritime centre and consideration should be given to the establishment of a shipyard in that community. That is the unavoidable conclusion to which we have come after a thorough examination of the problem.
The constituency I represent in this dignified chamber is, as everybody knows, one of those regions affected by economic stagnation. I will admit that commendable efforts have been made in the past, particularly during the last season, by means of large winter works grants.
Thus, the city of Trois Pistoles ranked first in Quebec for its winter works program, thanks to indispensable co-operation by its civic representatives. As a matter of fact, all the mayors of the municipalities in the county I represent surely deserve to be commended for their initiative at the opportune time.
Hon. members of the house, first let us all admit that we meet here with the responsibility of giving the Canadian people the best possible government, that is the part we have to play, and also our responsibility. Indeed, did we not promise it to our voters, to all those men and women in our respective ridings, even before undertaking this task with a solemn oath to Her Majesty, our gracious and glorious Queen, Elizabeth II.
I am very far from agreeing with those who want another election to settle our

The Budget-Mr. Ouellet political problems in Canada. The attitude of those who try to abuse the masses by their sustained effort to rouse one family against the other in a fight based on linguistic, racial and religious prejudices and even go as far as to hold the public or political authority entirely-not to say solely-responsible for troubles which are inherent to our earthly life, such attitude cannot be accepted.
As I said a moment ago, such attitude tortures people and distorts active democratic principles because another federal election, in Quebec at this time, would I am sorry to say, just delight all those who could not care less about the present needs and responsibilities.
We have a tremendous task to carry out here for four years, or longer if needed. At the end of that period, this parliament will have, I hope, the satisfaction of handing over to those who will form the twenty seventh parliament better conditions than the ones it inherited.
Furthermore, from the Macdonald-Cartier administration in 1867 down to the present time, Canada has profited by its politicians' solicitude. In every period, our Canadian people have freely recorded their epic events as well as their tragedies.
As I am now more fully aware of your kindness, hon. gentlemen, here is another remark which I would like to submit to your serious consideration.
The constituency which I represent is bounded on the north by the St. Lawrence and on the south by New Brunswick. This constituency is part of the senatorial division called Gulf, which is represented since July 1955 by a Canadian of Irish extraction. This hon. senator was a member of this house for 30 years and he is a valuable man in his political party because he is quite devoted to each and everyone. We must say that about him.
I shall therefore raise the following matter, which is of great concern to me, and I should like if possible to call the attention of government members, of Liberal members, to it, because it is serious and urgent.
Since the beginning of this century, the party in office at present has ruled over, or rather has controlled the appointments to the Senate for 43 out of the last 64 years.
As far as Acadians are concerned, I wonder why the Liberals have not treated fairly those fine Canadians who, moreover, support the Liberal party both at the federal and at the provincial levels? Shall we have to wait for another administration in Canada to get an answer, a solution? No, it would be really sad, even tragic. I do believe that we deserve another Sir Charles Tupper in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, if I talk like that, it is to claim fair representation for the Acadians in the Senate and also to solemnly state that I am not a separatist; I do not want to forsake, spurn or reject my compatriots in the other provinces of Canada. I feel that the confederation sanctioned by the Macdonald-Cartier ministry has until now justified the hopes of men who know the value of peace, peace within ourselves and with others.
Some might consider this statement rather daring, but it is a matter of deep faith and hope. Yes, we have our political independence in Canada. What we must still get is our economic independence, because we are under the domination of foreign, especially American, capital.
As I say, if there is a minority that we of Quebec must hold dear-in fact, our past attitude is not too glorious in that respect- it is certainly the Acadians. Have the most ardent nationalists of our province held a dialogue with French Canadians outside Quebec? Do they realize now that those who hurt them the most are the selfish Canadians who commit the sin known to anyone who has read Genesis, that of Cain, the hateful man who refused to show brotherly love to Abel.
In New Brunswick, where 40 per cent of the people are of Acadian origin, the premier who is an an Acadian himself has a hard time giving his people satisfactory economic conditions. We Quebeckers must throw in our lot with these admirable fellow citizens.
I am most pleased to tell you that I have had many opportunities to meet the people of northern New Brunswick where I have many relatives and friends. As I came to know them and their area, I rapidly formed a lasting friendship with those noble people, the most loyal subjects of Canada. These people constitute, in my opinion, one of the greatest treasures of our national inheritance.
I believe that everyone here no matter what part of this vast country he comes from, can acknowledge that I speak the truth. They settled here over 360 years ago and their unrivalled history is that of a people which would not disappear. Acadians, my cousins, my brothers, the Canadian confederation must be for you the subject of your most noble hopes.
Incidentally, I long for the day when we have a road, a highway connecting my county, from the St. Lawrence river to Moncton, the metropolis of the Acadians; a road which would go, for instance, from Bic, the centre of farm unionism, mutualism, co-operatism, in the lower St. Lawrence region, the Switzerland of lower Quebec, adorned by the Ile-au-Massacre, a memento of our civilization, would be an ideal starting point

towards the land of Evangeline. Such a motor trip would be for me, I dare say, a heavenly ride.
Mr. Speaker, may I exhort, even beg the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen), the Solicitor General (Mr. MacNaught); the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud), the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) to get together in order to promote the official recognition of the French language in New Brunswick before July 1, 1967.
In fact, recently we learned that the hon. member for lies de la Madeleine, stronghold of the Acadians, was appointed minister in the federal cabinet to administer the Department of Forestry. So it is in order to congratulate the holder of this office, without forgetting to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). No doubt, it was a nice surprise for the population of that constituency established in 1947.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a final appeal in favour of the rights of democracy in Canada.
Canadian democracy should not be used exclusively for political purposes where strength, trickery and profit too supersede the love of peace, justice and liberty. Let us face it, the power of Canada resides primarily in the soundness of its domestic markets. What are we doing for the economic and financial independence of the Canadian family? Have we, here in Canada, a policy concerning the Canadian family? We are unfortunately going ahead very tremulously in that regard.
In 1950, the federal government was more than making ends meet; it showed a surplus, with less than $2J billion for the year. This year it is asking for more than $7 billion. Therefore, the budget has nearly tripled in 15 years.
I am a member from Quebec province. What is happening there? Well, if we go back a few years, we find that at that time, the provincial government could get along on less than $500 million a year-more than that, it succeeded in reducing its public debt; today the provincial government expenditures reach a billion and a half.
The government's share has tripled, that is, it has tripled in Ottawa, and tripled in Quebec; the municipalities and the school boards, in the last 15 years, have had a similar experience. However, the income of the Quebec family, the rural family specially, has not tripled, no, never. Yet, we, the federal members, have seen our salary tripled, while that of the Quebec members has quadrupled since the war.
I realize that these facts are not very interesting. Nevertheless, I think that we must
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey straighten out things if we are to discharge our duty honourably here.
It seems to me, for instance, that any family concern, whatever it may be, should be protected and should also get some assistance. The family is the main cell or the basic cell of society.
Do not our family allowances, as they are nowadays in 1964, condemn our political system? We claim that we are always supporting the values of Christian civilization. Does not capitalism, through its abuses, expose us at present to the disorders and ruin which are brought about by bolshevism?
Let us be practical. A new alignment is required at this time because we are choking in a materialistic atmosphere. Canada with its human resources of all races, with the superabundance of its natural resources, our national natural resources, has been endowed by Providence for our welfare, that is the welfare of all Canadians over and above everything. Yes, Canada must provide for each family everything that a national birthright can guarantee. Therefore, let us fully dedicate ourselves right now to the imperatives of our time.
The one you have just heard is trying to speak on behalf of the man in the fields. I do not wish to hold any party or any member in check by the stand I am taking here.
I do not claim to be here for ever either; besides there is nothing permanent in this world. I come from the hinterland to make a heartfelt appeal to this dignified and majestic chamber and in so doing, I think I am the faithful voice, at least I earnestly hope so, of dozens of generations which have lived peacefully on the banks of the majestic St. Lawrence river.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened in relative quietness for the last two weeks to the debate on the supplementary estimates I welcome this opportunity to take a more vocal part in the deliberations of the house. Indeed, remembering the rather strange atmosphere that prevailed in the house during the last few weeks, I hope there is nothing in my speech that may do anything to reintroduce that type of ill will which we can do very well without in the house.
Certainly, Mr. Speaker, when I voice the opinion that possibly the economy of Canada is on the march once again, I am sure I have the full support of all hon. members of the house. The fact is that unemployment is practically non-existent in some parts of the country, and in others it is at its lowest point in many, many years.
Almost daily, presidents of our large corporations are tabling their financial reports

The Budget-Mr. Mackasey showing record profits, and our experts are predicting not only a greater share of the export market but that the present boom might very well continue into 1965.
I have not been long in the house, but long enough to witness the presentation of two budgets, and I may say that possibly this latter budget is but a continuation or an appendix of the first one presented by the Minister of Finance. I remember taking part in the budget debate last year when I predicted that some of the less noticeable parts in the budget would help the Canadian economy long after some of its more controversial aspects passed into oblivion. I can give one prime example of such a hidden factor in the minister's first budget. I refer, for instance, to the obvious and perhaps unexpected success of our auto parts industry as a result, not only of the first budget, but of enlightened legislation introduced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to support that budget.
The Financial Post of April 4 had an article headed "Car parts spreading prosperity all over". The article lists possibly a dozen or more small, independent, Canadian auto parts manufacturing firms which will have to expand because they are in the happy predicament of having more orders than they can fill with their present facilities.
Appearing elsewhere in the same issue of that newspaper is a table showing that last year we exported almost four times as many auto parts as in any year previously. Another article in that newspaper, in the same issue, written by Knowlton Nash in Washington, has a headline which reads, "U.S. twitches over our auto exports ... Ottawa plan seems to be working". This article outlines some of the things that are well known to most of us, for instance, that General Motors will be spending $120 million to build auto and truck assembly plants, and parts plants in Canada, and that Chrysler Corporation predicts that within 20 years their facilities and factories all over the world would be getting most of their more important parts from Canada.
American Motors Corporation is increasing its purchases of auto parts from Canada, especially bumpers, headlights, transmission parts and wheel covers, and the article further points out that the McCord Corporation of Detroit has placed orders for 100,000 radiators in Canada for the U.S. market in 1965.
There are many other examples in this article, which I do not intend to read into the record at this time, but one thing which did catch my fancy was the tribute paid to this legislation, to this boom in the auto parts industry, by a representative of the ;Ford Motor Company, who voiced cautiously
IMr. Mackasey.]
his approval of the plan and who indicated that the Ford Motor Company would soon be part and parcel of it. I think that tickled my fancy, and what I am sure will appeal to all non-partisan members of the house, is the fact he referred to the plan as the Drury plan. This puts a stamp of approval on it by the automobile parts manufacturers.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would be false to myself and the party I represent if I were to say or to intimate that all was well with the Canadian economy. As a matter of fact, many pockets of chronic unemployment that exist across the country are a source of concern to all of us, and perhaps even more so to me because I come from la belle province du Quebec. I feel very strongly about this problem because I think it is one of the contributing factors to the strength of the separatist movement in Quebec.
As a resident for 42 years of that province, as one who has had the privilege of breaking bread with French Canadians, as one who respects their traditions, language and culture, I feel strongly that the separatist movement could not stand alone on its emotional appeal to the French Canadians. Coupled with the tendency towards separatism was the despair and resentment that is a byproduct, and a bad by-product, of chronic unemployment. Picture, if you will, Mr. Speaker, the undue publicity this movement gets outside the province of Quebec. I usually go home at the week end. Later I pick up the papers in the parliamentary reading room on Mondays, Tuesdays and Wednesdays, and on reading them I do not recognize the province of Quebec where I have just spent two days. But I do feel that many irresponsible leaders in French Canada, leaders in politics, leaders in the newspaper world, leaders in our different organizations, are harnessing and using this movement for their own selfish short term gains. So, like everybody else in this chamber, I would welcome the disappearance of chronic unemployment in Canada.
I was not in the house earlier today when the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) spoke very eloquently, I understand, but I appreciate the sentiments he expressed toward the province of Quebec and as to the necessity for tolerance and understanding in this country. In my view, Mr. Speaker, we were all elected to this house because we were supposed to be 265 people with intelligence, tolerance and the ability to see the other man's point of view.
There is one last article in the Financial Post to which I should like to refer, and it touches on a different subject. It is written by a lawyer, John McDonald, Q.C., a very prominent person in the economic field. I am

interested in the article not because I want to refer to its contents, although I think some of the economists in this house and would-be economists would do well to look at it. I am interested basically in the headline which is in these words: "How to Buy Back Canada". It is particularly significant to me because I think it represents to us a fact about which many deep thinking Canadians are perturbed and worried. I refer to the fact that daily more of our heritage and our children's birthright disappears into the hands of friendly but foreign interests.
I pay tribute to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) this evening for having at least paid some attention to this problem. Whether or not we agree with the method he employed is another matter. Certainly economists, like lawyers, are a breed that tend to disagree. But the important thing is that the Minister of Finance is aware of the problem and is searching desperately for some solution, in the same way that many other Canadians are, as Mr. McDonald indicated. Before I go on record in the mind of any member of the house as being against foreign capital, may I say I think it is our duty to encourage foreign capital to come into Canada, but I think that the type of foreign capital we need is that which comes into our country in the form of loans or debentures, the type of capital which comes into this country under a contract specifically stating when we can pay the money back and at what interest. This country can ill afford any further domination of its economic future.
If, as some cynics seem to feel, the time is perhaps even too late to win back any part of our economic control, there is one field where I believe we can do something. I refer to the gradual domination of our field of communications by outside interests. I feel very strongly on this point because in my view communications and culture are synonomous in the world of today, and what would Canada be without its Canadian indentity and Canadian culture? I think history will at some time in the future pay tribute to the part that French Canada has played in retaining the French culture and therefore a Canadian culture.
The fields of communication which I believe should be kept purely and simply allCanadian are radio, television, our daily newspapers and our periodicals. Living as we do next door to a nation which for the most part shares our language, our common heritage and our democratic principles we are faced with the danger of losing control of our culture and communications in the same way we have lost control over so many of our industries. That is why I am a strong advocate of the C.B.C. While I do not believe
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey that the C.B.C. is above criticism, that it does not need reform periodically or a new financial administration, I shudder when I see well meaning members stand up in the house and, by their questions, their suggestions and their pleas try to reduce the C.B.C. to a pale carbon copy of our private radio and television interests. In my view the C.B.C. was one of the greatest single forces and factors in the emergence of Canada as a nation, and when and if the C.B.C. is watered down to that carbon copy to which I have referred I believe we will have witnessed-

Our expert in lariats is back again. Happy birthday.
I feel that when that day comes we will have begun the acceleration of the end of Canada as a country. I feel just as strongly about our daily newspapers. Who would be left to help us fight against the constant encroachment into Canadian industry?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Conservative party.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are not the only country which has had this problem. France recognized it in 1944. Many members of the house know that France lost a very important segment of its daily newspapers before the last war. In 1944 France introduced legislation and I should like to read into the record one clause:
All owners, partners, shareholders, silent partners, financial backers or other persons financially interested in a publication must be of French nationality.
This is the type of positive clearcut action that we need to protect our communications in Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Give us your opinion of Time and Reader's Digest while you are at it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Our great friend is back again. One rather looks for hon. members on that side to have enough courtesy to keep quiet while a member is speaking. I may get to Time and Reader's Digest.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You were reading your speech so well that I thought you needed a few interruptions.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has indicated its intention to introduce

The Budget-Mr. Mackasey legislation at this session of parliament to help Canadian periodicals. It is designed to make advertising in Canadian periodicals more attractive than advertising in American periodicals. It is a well known fact that most of our periodicals are doomed to extinction unless some financial assistance comes their way. That is why I believe that Reader's Digest and Time must not be exempt from the proposed legislation. I feel very strongly that Reader's Digest and Time magazine are American publications, have always been American publications and fully intend to remain American publications. It is my strong view that so far as the editorial content of a magazine is concerned the nationality of the people who write the editorials should be the criterion, whether or not a magazine is Canadian or American. The fact that it is printed in Canada, Mr. Speaker, is incidental, and it is the source from which the dictation of its editorial policy comes that is a deciding factor. I cannot, for the life of me, see how two United States magazines, owned by United States capital, can consider themselves to be Canadian publications merely because they contain four pages of Canadian material.
I often wonder what the policy of these particular magazines would be, if they were forced at some date in the future when our two countries may not see eye to eye on a common problem, to take a stand. Would they take a stand for the Canadian point of view or the United States point of view? May I just allay the fears of the many readers of Time and Reader's Digest in this country? I fully believe that if the legislation is extended to include Reader's Digest and Time, these two excellent magazines will continue on the newstands because they are basically excellent magazines. We have other excellent magazines that are out and out United States publications and make no pretence about being Canadian. I could cite as examples, Saturday Evening Post, Fortune and many other magazines. I feel that I must, here and now, reserve my right to speak again when this legislation is brought before the house.
I feel, in view of the situation in relation to the province of Quebec, the time has come when our newspapers, periodicals and opinion formers, our professors, teachers, indeed all Canadians must take a good look at the problem of being Canadian today. We must now put political expediency aside; we must put regionalism aside, indeed even politics aside, if this country is to meet the challenge that lies before it. It is time for the members of this house to show some of the qualities which it was presumed they possessed when they came into this house. It is time that

English speaking members showed some responsibility outside the house when they are discussing Quebec, and it is also time some of our French Canadian members used a little discretion, a little more restraint when speaking inside the house.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that it was suggested to me a few hours ago that, when I suggested the possible inclusion of Time and Reader's Digest in this proposed legislation, I did so because I represented hidden interests. I can assure you, sir, and the house that nothing is further from the truth. Like so many other members here I came to this house with no special talents;
I represent no wealth, no pressure groups, but I do represent 90,000 Canadians and I have the courage of my convictions and a willingness to express them in this house.
I am one Canadian who is prepared to stand up and be counted when Canada is at stake.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We
have heard, Mr. Speaker, during the resumption of this budget debate a complete review of all sorts of adjectives applied to this budget. In fact, I sympathized with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) when he was attempting to find some new ones. I must say that I thought his efforts sounded a little laboured.
In so far as this budget is concerned, I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) must feel fairly secure, at least secure in the knowledge he is not going to win any Oscar. After all, we understand that there is a performance in some other place tonight in which Oscars are being awarded. I do not believe last year's performance or this year's will give the minister any nomination for that award. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the minister last year reminded me a little of the hot-shot rookie coming up to the national hockey league. He goes out for the first game and, with a great burst of speed cuts around the goal but, somehow or other, he steps on a piece of tape and you know where he lands. This year, he has come out a second time, but much more cautiously, and may suffer from that a bit.
In any event, let us look at this budget. Without anticipating the debate that may follow on some of the resolutions, there is one item I should like to bring to the attention of the house. I refer to paragraph 7 of the income tax resolution under which a taxpayer, in computing his income, may have amounts expended by him in relation to the objection to his assessment, or an appeal from an assessment, and shall include in computing income any costs recovered in respect thereof. I hope the minister has some detailed explanation of the limitations that

will be imposed on this provision. I hope my fellow lawyers are not going to take me to task, or even the accountants, but if severe limitations are not imposed on this provision I can foresee one big field day.
Who is going to say what are the costs of filing an objection to an assessment, or of prosecuting an appeal? I must say, therefore, we will undoubtedly get a clarification of this point. When we merely say that the taxpayers are going to be allowed the amount expended by them in this fashion, I think we are glossing it over. I feel we are going to get a lot of restrictions indicated by the minister when we come to a discussion of this resolution. Let us not look at this as a whole bag of goodies, because they just are not going to be there.
I should like to refer now to the other matter I had in mind. If we look at the estimates we know that the Minister of Finance indicated that in 1964-65 he expected a budgetary deficit of $402 million. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Now-lan) has indicated quite clearly, as have a number of other hon. members, that in order to get down to this figure of $402 million the minister is going to have a windfall this year of some $170 million as a result of an acceleration in the payment of corporate income tax. This, of course, is something that has to be examined in proper perspective, and the indications are that, if it were not for this sum the deficit would be back to $585 million. I am not suggesting that we should be shouting for higher and higher deficits. As a matter of fact, when I listened to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) I thought that apparently that wing of the party says: We could not care less about the size of the deficit; spend and spend.
On the other hand, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) expressed his regret this evening that the minister had not imposed a tax cut. I do not know how these hon. members intend to get the best of both worlds.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That would be a good way to get a deficit, though.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) was not talking about tax cuts. His idea was just that we should spend the money. The hon. member for Greenwood did not have much to say about spending programs. He wanted the minister to cut taxes.
In any event, there is an item of $14,250,000 which I think the minister has tucked away neatly. I do not think this item appears where it should appear and where it will, ultimately appear. I refer to loans. He has made a loan
The Budget-Mr. Lambert to the C.B.C. of $14,250,000 for capital projects. But how does he anticipate that this will be repaid? This corporation, unlike Atomic Energy of Canada, for example, is not a profit-making crown corporation. The C.B.C. takes anywhere from $75 million to $95 million from the treasury each year to meet the obligations imposed on it by the Broadcasting Act. Yet the minister lends the corporation more than $14 million. We would certainly like to know how the corporation intends to repay it. I am sure it is not the president of the corporation, or the vice president, or any of the board of directors who are going to repay the loan. Somewhere along the line, two or three years hence, the minister will have to write off this loan and the amount will then have to go on the expenditure side.
I think, therefore, we should raise the amount of estimated expenditure by this $14,250,000.
There is not much time left before ten o'clock and I had intended to speak about two points relating to sales tax. However, I think I will leave them until we are discussing the resolutions on excise tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You will have a hard time doing that. There are none.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, the application of sales tax to production machinery came into effect last year. I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will grant me a little indulgence; I do not intend to discourse on matters which have been covered before. I think the minister is aware of this problem. It was raised last year and I indicated it would arise, particularly in respect of goods acquired prior to June 13 but delivered subsequently. We face a real problem in the city of Edmonton. As a result of a tender, the city entered into an agreement for the purchase of a steam turbine generator at a cost of some $2,200,000. The minister indicates, in the correspondence which I have read, that unfortunately the city will have to pay the sales tax because they did not buy this machinery for re-sale to someone else-in other words, they were not committed to pass it on to someone else at a firm price. But this turbine will not be delivered and installed before 1965. Because the city bought it for its own use for the production of electricity within the community, it now has to pay the sales tax. Strangely enough, if the city had bought this turbine through an intermediary who was importing it into the country from Britain, there would have been no sales tax.
I confess I find some difficulty in understanding the logic of the position. If this turbine had been bought by an intermediary for the city of Edmonton for delivery there would have been no liability for sales tax. Yet because the city buys it, and because part

The Budget-Mr. Lambert of it is made in Canada, sales tax is to be charged. I submit that the explanations given by the minister last year, the nature of the hon. gentleman's speech, indicated that this steam turbine would not be subject to sales tax. Nevertheless, in the cold light of administration, we now find that the tax has been imposed.
With respect to loans to university students, I would draw the minister's attention to the proposal put to him and to members of this house by the Canadian union of students who prefer some sort of scholarship bursary grant based on scholastic attainment and on need. As to this whole matter of interest free loans, it will be most instructive to see how the banks will, in fact, administer them.
I was gratified to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) with regard to Time and Reader's Digest. Reader's Digest is, I think, harmless with respect to the pressure it could bring to bear, but I can assure the hon. member that if there ever was a difference of opinion on policy between Canada and the United States all he needs to read is the editorializing which is done in the other publication and he will see just where the pressure is applied. I believe the proposal which the government is now making is just one which will lead to the rich getting richer and the poor getting poorer. What is being done is to enshrine in legislation the precise anomalies which existed previously, shutting out competition
from Time and Reader's Digest and building a beautiful protective fence around them so that the other publications are in a worse position. The advantage about which we have complained is now to be protected by legislation. For this reason I think the government should take another look at this proposal. I do not approve this principle of exempting particular publications. It is like picking out one taxpayer and saying to him: We intend to let you get by; you do not need to pay this particular type of income tax. Or: We intend to give you a particular exemption, or an accelerated rate of depreciation. To my mind this is a bad tax principle and the sooner the government can get rid of it the better off we shall be.
May I call it ten o'clock?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to ask the leader of the house what business we shall have before us on Wednesday and the rest of the week, if he is able to tell us.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We shall, of course, be completing the budget debate tomorrow. As to Wednesday and the rest of the week, and maybe the beginning of next week, I hope to be in a position to make a full announcement some time tomorrow afternoon.
It being two minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, April 14, 1984
